title: Preface
text:
What this guide helps you do
Statistical analysis helps us learn from data while recognizing uncertainty. Choosing a test is one part of that work. We also need a clear question, suitable data, an understanding of the study design, and an honest explanation of what the findings support.
This free guide from Complex Data Insights (CDI) helps you move from a dataset to an output you understand and can defend.
Examples will draw on education, agriculture, business, and biology. Synthetic datasets will support learning without implying real-world evidence.

title: Preface
text:
The CDI approach
Your question → Your inputs → Ask AI → Work through → Check evidence → Answer with limitations.

Your question: State what you want to learn and why it matters.
Your inputs: Identify the outcome, comparison, independent units, and study design.
Ask AI: Share the relevant context and request an explanation, possible approach, or help with code. Ask it to identify missing information.
Work through: Run the analysis and inspect the data, code, and outputs.
Check evidence: Verify calculations, assumptions, documentation, and whether the interpretation matches the result.
Answer with limitations: Explain the finding in context, including uncertainty and what the design cannot establish.

You can follow the same workflow without an AI tool by using the explanations, scripts, and references directly.

title: Preface
text:
Use AI. Check the evidence.
AI can help explain a method, draft code, troubleshoot an error, or improve the wording of a result. Its suggestions still require review. A confident explanation may overlook paired observations, missing data, confounding, or an unsuitable model.
Start with your own question. Give AI enough context to assess the design, then check its response against your data and the relevant method chapter.
For example:

I want to compare assessment scores between two groups of learners. Help me identify the outcome, independent unit, and target estimate. Ask whether the observations are independent, paired, or clustered before suggesting a method. Explain what information is missing and what I should verify. Do not invent results.

Keep a record of consequential AI suggestions and the decisions you made after checking them. Use synthetic data or appropriately de-identified summaries when seeking help, and follow the applicable permissions for confidential data.
You remain responsible for the analysis and the claims you make from it.

The project keeps scripts in scripts/R/, scripts/python/, and scripts/bash/. R and Python support statistical analysis and plotting; Bash supports setup and workflow checks. A chapter may use whichever language best suits the example, without duplicating every analysis in all three languages.

title: Preface
text:
What makes a finding defensible?
Before sharing an analysis, ask:

Does the method address my original question and study design?
Can I trace the result to the data and code that produced it?
Have I checked relevant assumptions and explained important limitations?
Have I reported the size and uncertainty of the result, rather than only a p-value?
Could another person reproduce the analysis from the supplied materials?

A small p-value does not establish a large or useful effect. A large p-value does not establish that no effect exists. Interpretation requires the estimate, uncertainty, context, and design.

title: From Questions to Statistical Methods

1. Your question
A statistical analysis begins with a question. Before choosing a test or asking AI for code, describe what you want to learn, what you measured, and how the observations were collected.
By the end of this chapter, you should be able to write an analysis question, identify your outcome and unit of observation, recognize paired data, and justify a starting method.
Suppose a training program offers two teaching approaches. You want to know:
This question identifies the outcome (assessment score), comparison (A versus B), and target estimate (the difference in population mean scores).
A useful question states:
Avoid starting with “Which test gives a significant result?” Choose the question and analysis before inspecting which method produces the smallest p-value.

title: From Questions to Statistical Methods
text:
3. Check the study design

Independent groups
Different people, plots, or other units belong to each group. In the training example, each learner contributes one score and belongs to one approach.


Paired measurements
The same person is measured before and after training, or observations are explicitly matched. Analyze the within-pair differences for a paired mean comparison.
Two columns with the same number of rows are not automatically paired. Each pair must have a meaningful link.


Repeated or clustered observations
Examples include weekly scores from each learner, learners within classrooms, and several leaves measured from each plant. Measurements from the same learner, classroom, or plant may be correlated.
Do not treat every measurement as an independent replicate. A simple two-group test may be unsuitable; the analysis may require aggregation justified by the question, or a model that accounts for clustering or repeated measurements.






Independence comes from the design



A histogram or normality test cannot establish independence. Check how participants were sampled, assigned, measured, and grouped.

text:
5. Use AI and check its suggestions
Write your own question and input summary first. Then ask AI to explain a possible method and identify missing information.

Example prompt

I am comparing assessment scores between two teaching approaches. Each learner belongs to one approach and contributes one score from 0 to 100. My target estimate is the population mean score for A minus that for B. Explain whether Welch’s t-test is suitable. Ask about sampling, assignment, clustering, sample sizes, missing values, and unusual observations before recommending an analysis. State the assumptions, alternatives, and limits of the interpretation. Do not invent results.

Use synthetic examples or appropriately de-identified summaries when discussing data with an AI tool. Do not include identifying or confidential records without authorization.


Check the response







AI suggestion
Your check




“Use a paired t-test.”
Are these the same learners measured twice or genuinely matched pairs?


“Use a t-test because the outcome is numerical.”
Does the design support independent units, and is a mean difference the intended estimate?


“The sample is large, so assumptions do not matter.”
Are there clusters, influential observations, or sampling problems that sample size cannot fix?


“A significant difference proves the teaching approach works.”
Does the design support a causal interpretation? Could selection or confounding explain the association?


“Use Mann–Whitney to test the medians.”
What assumptions would allow a location or median interpretation?



AI can help draft code, explain output, and suggest checks. Run and inspect the code yourself. Verify documentation for unfamiliar functions and keep a record of consequential analysis decisions.

title: From Questions to Statistical Methods
text:
6. Write your analysis plan
For the training example, a short plan could read:

We will compare assessment scores between Approach A and Approach B using the difference in means, defined as A minus B. Each learner contributes one observation. We will examine group sizes, missing scores, score distributions, and unusual observations before analysis. If an independent mean comparison is appropriate, we will use Welch’s t-test and report the estimated mean difference, its 95% confidence interval, and the two-sided p-value. Interpretation will account for how learners were recruited and assigned to approaches.

Specify any adjustment variables, subgroup analyses, and multiple comparisons before examining their results. If the plan changes, record the reason and distinguish planned from exploratory work.

title: From Questions to Statistical Methods
text:
7. Verify and explain
Before proceeding, answer these questions in your own words:

What is my outcome, and what type of variable is it?
What does one row represent? What is the independent unit?
Are observations independent, paired, repeated, or clustered?
What quantity do I want to estimate, including its direction and units?
Why does my proposed method fit that question and design?
What could limit the interpretation, even if the p-value is small?


Try it
A farm records crop yield from 12 plots before and after a soil treatment. Each plot has a unique identifier and contributes both measurements.

Is this an independent or paired comparison?
What quantity would you estimate?
What limits a claim that the treatment caused any observed change?







Check your reasoning





The measurements are paired by plot. A useful target is the mean within-plot yield change, defined as after minus before and expressed in the yield units. A paired t-test may be appropriate if the plot differences meet its conditions and plots provide independent replication. Without an appropriate comparison group or design, weather, season, and other changes could explain the observed difference. Pairing alone does not establish causation.

Treating multiple measurements from one unit as independent replicates.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
1. Your question
A sample gives us information about a larger population, but another sample would usually produce a different result. Statistical inference uses data and assumptions to estimate population quantities and assess uncertainty.
This chapter helps you distinguish the size of a finding from the strength of evidence against a statistical hypothesis.
We observe scores for a sample of learners. The sample mean is available to calculate; the population mean is the unknown quantity we want to estimate.
Inference depends on how the sample was obtained. A narrow confidence interval cannot correct a biased sample or an inappropriate design.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
What is the mean assessment score among learners in a training program, and how precisely can we estimate it?










Term
Meaning
Training example




Population
The group the question concerns
All eligible learners in the program


Sample
The units actually observed
The learners whose scores we collect


Parameter
A population quantity
Population mean assessment score

Sample mean assessment score

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
2. Start with the estimate
An estimate answers “How much?” Examples include:

A mean score of 72 points.
A mean difference of 5 points between groups.
A pass proportion of 0.80, or 80%.
A difference in pass proportions of 0.10, or 10 percentage points.

State the direction and units. For a comparison defined as A minus B, a positive mean difference means A has the higher estimated mean.
An effect size describes the magnitude of a difference or relationship. It may be expressed in the original units, such as score points, or on a standardized scale. Original units often make practical meaning easier to judge.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
3. Distinguish spread from precision
Standard deviation (SD) describes variation among individual observations. Standard error (SE) describes the sampling variability of an estimator under the assumed design and model.
For the mean of independent observations with a common finite variance, the usual estimated SE is:
\[
SE(\bar{x}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Here, \(s\) is the sample SD and \(n\) is the sample size. This simple formula is not appropriate for every design, such as unaccounted repeated measurements or clustering.
If the SD stays similar, collecting more independent observations generally reduces the SE. It does not necessarily reduce the variation among individuals.






More rows do not always mean more independent information



Ten measurements from each of ten learners are not equivalent to one measurement from each of 100 independent learners. The analysis must account for the relationship among measurements.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
4. Understand a confidence interval
A confidence interval combines an estimate with uncertainty calculated using a specified procedure.
For a population mean, the usual one-sample t interval is:
\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
The multiplier is a t-distribution critical value for a two-sided 95% interval. Its suitability depends on the design and distributional conditions. The method chapters explain these conditions in context.

Worked example
Suppose a synthetic sample has:



Quantity
Value




Independent learners
25


Sample mean
72 points


Sample SD
10 points


Estimated SE
2 points


t critical value, 24 degrees of freedom
Approximately 2.064



The interval is:
\[
72 \pm 2.064 \times 2 \approx [67.87,\;76.13]
\]
We estimate the population mean as 72 points, with a 95% confidence interval from approximately 67.87 to 76.13 points.
The 95% describes the long-run coverage of the procedure: under its assumptions, intervals calculated from repeated samples would contain the fixed population mean about 95% of the time.
It does not mean that 95% of individual learners score within this interval. It also does not assign a 95% probability to the fixed population mean lying inside this particular observed interval.


Verify the calculation in R
This code uses summary statistics for illustration. It does not check the underlying scores or study design.
The following blocks display excerpts from the complete R script. Quarto does not execute them. Copy the script into scripts/R/ and run it from the repository root:
Rscript scripts/R/02-statistical-inference.R
The script uses base R and prints both the confidence interval and the test result. No additional R packages are required.
# Summary statistics for the synthetic example.
n <- 25
sample_mean <- 72
sample_sd <- 10

# Estimate precision and calculate the t-based interval.
standard_error <- sample_sd / sqrt(n)
critical_value <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
margin <- critical_value * standard_error

c(
  mean = sample_mean,
  standard_error = standard_error,
  lower_95 = sample_mean - margin,
  upper_95 = sample_mean + margin
)
Expected output, rounded: mean = 72; SE = 2; lower limit = 67.87; upper limit = 76.13.
The code is displayed for you to run in R; rendering this chapter does not execute it.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
5. State the hypotheses
Suppose the reference mean score is 70 points. A two-sided test asks whether the population mean differs from that value.

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The population mean equals 70 points.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)): The population mean differs from 70 points.

The hypotheses concern the population parameter. The observed sample mean need not equal the reference value even when the null hypothesis is true.
Choose a one-sided alternative only when it is justified by the question and specified before inspecting the results. Do not switch direction after seeing the data.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
6. Interpret the p-value
A p-value is the probability, under the null hypothesis and the test’s other assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic in the direction or directions specified by the test.
In the synthetic example:
\[
t = \frac{72 - 70}{2} = 1
\]
For a two-sided one-sample t-test with 24 degrees of freedom, the p-value is approximately 0.327.
# Run after the preceding summary-statistic code.
reference_mean <- 70

t_statistic <- (sample_mean - reference_mean) / standard_error
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_statistic), df = n - 1)

c(t = t_statistic, df = n - 1, p_value = p_value)
This result does not provide strong evidence against a population mean of 70 under the test assumptions. The 95% confidence interval also includes 70.







A p-value does not tell you…
What to examine instead




The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The test assumptions and broader evidence; hypothesis probabilities require a different inferential framework


The probability that the result occurred “by chance”
The specific probability defined under the null model


How large or useful the effect is
The estimate, units, uncertainty, and practical context


Whether the study design establishes causation
Sampling, assignment, confounding, and other design features


Whether a large p-value proves no effect
The interval and whether important effects remain compatible with the data and model

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
7. Understand thresholds and errors
A significance level, often written \(\alpha\), is a threshold specified for a testing procedure. A common choice is 0.05, but its appropriateness depends on the purpose and consequences of the decision.







Concept
Meaning




Type I error
Rejecting a true null hypothesis


Type II error
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis


Power
Probability of rejecting the null for a specified alternative, design, and test



For a valid test, the significance level controls the Type I error rate under its assumptions. It is not the probability that a particular reported finding is false.
A p-value of 0.049 and one of 0.051 provide very similar evidence. Avoid making sharply different scientific claims solely because they fall on different sides of a threshold.
For matching two-sided tests and confidence intervals constructed using the same method, a 95% interval excluding the null value corresponds to rejection at the 0.05 level. This correspondence need not hold when methods, adjustments, or alternatives differ.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
8. Separate statistical and practical importance
Suppose a comparison estimates a mean score difference of 0.4 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.2 to 0.6 points. The interval excludes zero, but a difference this small may have little practical value.
Another comparison estimates 5 points, with an interval from -1 to 11 points. That interval includes zero and potentially important positive differences. The result is uncertain; it does not establish no difference.
Define a meaningful difference using the subject area, measurement scale, costs, and intended decision. Specify it before examining results where possible. Establishing equivalence requires a suitable design and analysis; an ordinary nonsignificant test is insufficient.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
section: 9. Use AI and check its suggestions
text:
9. Use AI and check its suggestions

Example prompt

A synthetic sample of 25 independent learners has a mean score of 72 and a sample SD of 10. The reference population mean is 70. Explain the SE, a two-sided 95% t confidence interval, and the two-sided one-sample t-test p-value. State the assumptions that cannot be checked from these summaries. Distinguish uncertainty about the population mean from variation among learner scores. Do not describe the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true.



Verify before using the explanation

Recalculate the SE: \(10 / \sqrt{25} = 2\).
Check the degrees of freedom: \(25 - 1 = 24\).
Check that the interval is centered on 72 and includes 70.
Check that the test statistic is 1 and the two-sided p-value is approximately 0.327.
Check that the interpretation addresses the population mean, not individual scores.
Ask which design and distributional assumptions remain unverified.

AI-generated precision is not evidence of correctness. Verify numbers and wording against the calculation and the method’s definition.

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
10. Report the finding
For this teaching example:

In the synthetic sample of 25 learners, the mean assessment score was 72 points (SD 10). The estimated population mean had a 95% t confidence interval of 67.87 to 76.13 points. A two-sided one-sample t-test against 70 points yielded \(t(24)=1.00\), \(p=0.327\). These data provide limited evidence against the reference mean under the test assumptions. The summary statistics alone do not allow assessment of sampling quality, independence, or unusual observations.

Keep the estimate and uncertainty central. Avoid reducing the report to “significant” or “not significant.”

title: Understanding Statistical Inference
text:
11. Check your understanding
A report states:

The p-value was 0.18, so there is an 18% probability that no difference exists.

What is wrong with this interpretation? What additional results would you request?






Check your reasoning





A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis and the test’s other assumptions. It does not give the probability that the null is true. Request the estimated difference, confidence interval, units, sample sizes, design, and relevant assumption checks. These help assess the magnitude, precision, and limitations of the finding.

title: Checking Data and Assumptions
text:
1. Your question and inputs
A test can run successfully on unsuitable data. Before calculating a p-value, check what each row represents, whether values make sense, and whether the proposed method matches the design.
This chapter uses synthetic assessment scores to demonstrate a basic checking workflow. It prepares you for the method chapters; it does not perform the final group comparison.
For this illustration, assume different learners contribute one score each and there is no classroom clustering. In an applied study, verify those facts from the study records.
There are 42 synthetic learners, 21 per approach. Each group contains 20 observed scores and one missing score. These data are separate from the summary-statistic illustration in Chapter 02.

3. Check missing data

Equal missing counts do not establish that missingness is harmless. For example, missing scores could come from learners who found the assessment especially difficult.
Ask why the values are missing, whether missingness relates to the outcome or predictors, and how excluding records changes the population represented by the analysis.
Do not replace missing scores with zero. Zero is a real score on this scale. Simple mean imputation also changes variability and can distort uncertainty. Select a missing-data approach appropriate to the question and plausible missingness process, and state its assumptions.
Here, the plots and summaries use observed scores only. This is a description of available data, not a justification for excluding missing scores from every subsequent inference.

title: Checking Data and Assumptions
text:
4. Check independence and pairing
Independence is supported by the sampling and measurement process, not established by a normality test.

Different independently sampled learners with one score each may support an independent comparison.
Before-and-after measurements on the same learners require a paired or repeated-measures approach.
Learners within classrooms may share conditions and have correlated outcomes.
Multiple measurements from one plant or participant are not automatically separate independent replicates.

If the design does not fit a simple independent test, address that before interpreting its output. A transformation or rank-based test does not remove dependence.

title: Checking Data and Assumptions
text:
5. Inspect plots within groups






Figure 3.1: Synthetic assessment scores by approach and normal Q-Q plots within each group. Horizontal spread in the left panel only separates points; Q-Q panels use different vertical ranges.



The left panel shows individual observations. Approach B has a wider spread. The horizontal positions within each group are visual offsets and do not encode learner order or another variable.
The Q-Q panels compare ordered scores with theoretical normal quantiles. Points approximately following a straight line are consistent with a roughly normal shape; systematic curves or large departures may indicate skewness, heavy tails, or unusual observations. Small samples provide limited information about distribution shape.
The synthetic points lie fairly close to their reference lines. This does not prove normality or validate the study design. The Q-Q panels have different vertical scales: compare shape there and use the left panel and SDs to compare spread.

Which distribution matters?







Proposed analysis
Relevant diagnostic target




One-sample t-test
Distribution of the numerical outcome


Independent-samples t-test
Distribution within each group


Paired t-test
Distribution of within-pair differences


Linear regression
Model residuals and their relationship to fitted values and predictors



For example, pooling two groups with different means can produce a misleading shape. For a paired test, examining the before and after distributions separately does not replace checking the differences.

title: Checking Data and Assumptions
text:
6. Understand assumptions in context

Normality
Normal-theory procedures may require approximately normal errors or observations for exact small-sample inference. Some mean-based procedures tolerate moderate departures under suitable conditions, but performance depends on sample size, balance, tail behavior, and influential observations.
Do not use a normality-test p-value as an automatic switch between tests. A small sample may fail to reveal an important departure; a large sample may detect a small departure with little practical consequence. Combine plots, design knowledge, and method-specific reasoning.


Variability
The observed SDs are approximately 6.97 points in A and 13.96 points in B. Equal sample sizes do not imply equal population variances. Welch’s independent-samples t-test accommodates unequal variances; it still requires an appropriate design and attention to distribution shape and influential observations.


Unusual values
A score of 100 may be valid. A score of 1000 is outside the stated scale and needs investigation. Being unusual does not by itself justify removal.
Verify source records, distinguish errors from valid extremes, and document any exclusion rule. If a valid value strongly affects the conclusion, consider a clearly described sensitivity analysis. Do not remove observations to obtain significance.


Relationships and residuals
Correlation and regression require additional checks. A scatterplot may reveal curvature, subgroups, or a single influential observation. Regression diagnostics may reveal nonlinearity, changing residual spread, or dependence over time. The relevant chapters develop these checks.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
1. Your question
We use 20 synthetic learner scores. The target estimate is the population mean minus 65, measured in score points. Positive values indicate a mean above the reference.
The reference is an illustrative fixed benchmark chosen before analysis. It is not a universal passing standard. The data reuse the 20 observed Approach A scores from Chapter 03 as a standalone teaching example; this does not justify ignoring that chapter’s missing scores in an applied analysis.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text: Does the population mean assessment score differ from a prespecified reference of 65 points?

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
2. When to use this method
Use a one-sample t-test when you have a numerical outcome from independent units and want to compare its population mean with a fixed reference.







Suitable question
Example




Does a mean differ from a benchmark?
Mean assessment score versus 65 points


Does a mean measurement differ from a specification?
Mean package weight versus 500 grams


Is a mean difference zero?
Paired differences analyzed as one numerical sample; see Chapter 06



If the reference is an estimate from another sample, treating it as fixed ignores its uncertainty. A two-sample comparison or another model may be appropriate. If your question concerns a proportion or a median, this test does not directly answer it.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
Let \(\mu\) denote the population mean and \(\mu_0=65\) the fixed reference.

Null hypothesis: \(H_0: \mu=65\).
Two-sided alternative: \(H_1: \mu\ne65\).
Estimated difference: \(\bar{x}-65\).

The test statistic expresses the difference in estimated standard errors:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}, \qquad df=n-1.
\]
For independent observations from a normal population, this statistic follows a t distribution under the null. Under other distributions, the accuracy of the approximation depends on sample size, shape, and tail behavior.
A two-sided test allows departures in either direction. Specify a one-sided alternative only when justified before looking at the scores.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
4. Check your data and assumptions







Check
What to establish




Independent units
One score per independently observed learner; no unaccounted classroom clustering


Appropriate sampling
A defensible connection between the sample and target population


Numerical scale
A mean is meaningful and units are consistent


Missingness
Missing scores and exclusions are understood and documented


Shape and unusual values
No severe skewness or influential extremes that make small-sample t inference unreliable


Reference
Benchmark is fixed, relevant, and chosen without searching for significance



Use individual-value plots and a normal Q-Q plot. At \(n=20\), shape and unusual observations deserve attention. A nonsignificant normality test does not establish normality. The script saves diagnostic plots for inspection after you run it.
No distributional diagnostic can establish independence or representative sampling. Review the study records as well as the scores.

5. Run the analysis

dat <- read.csv("data/example/04-assessment-scores.csv",
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

              conf.level = 0.95)

mean_difference <- mean(scores) - reference_mean
difference_ci <- fit$conf.int - reference_mean

  lower_95 = difference_ci[1],
  upper_95 = difference_ci[2])

7. Use AI and check its suggestions

I have 20 independent synthetic scores with mean 69.30 and SD approximately 6.97. The prespecified fixed reference is 65. Explain a two-sided one-sample t-test and distinguish the confidence interval for the population mean from the interval for the difference. Ask about sampling, independence, missingness, and distribution shape. Check the code against the supplied input rather than inventing scores. Do not interpret the result as proof that training caused an improvement.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
8. Report your finding

In this synthetic sample of 20 learners, the mean assessment score was 69.30 points (SD 6.97). The estimated difference from the prespecified reference of 65 was 4.30 points (95% CI 1.04 to 7.56). A two-sided one-sample t-test yielded \(t(19)=2.76\), \(p=0.0125\). Under the test assumptions, the results provide evidence that the population mean differs from the benchmark, with the estimate above it. The comparison does not establish a training effect, and practical importance depends on the educational context.

For an applied report, add the sampling process, relevant diagnostic findings, handling of missing data, and any deviations from the analysis plan.

title: One-Sample t-Test
text:
9. Common mistakes and alternatives







Problem
Better approach




Treating an estimated comparison-group mean as fixed
Account for both samples’ uncertainty


Treating repeated scores as independent
Use a paired or repeated-measures approach


Switching to a one-sided test after seeing the result
Retain the planned alternative; label later exploration


Removing a valid extreme score to obtain significance
Investigate and document it; consider a justified sensitivity analysis


Equating a small p-value with an important difference
Report the difference, interval, and context


Choosing a rank test solely because a normality test rejects
Consider the target quantity and assumptions of each alternative



For strong skewness or influential values, reassess the data, design, and inferential target. A transformation changes the scale and interpretation. A bootstrap interval for a mean can be useful under suitable sampling conditions but may perform poorly with very small samples or heavy tails. A signed-rank test has different assumptions and does not generally test the arithmetic mean. Obtain more independent information or specialist advice when the design or distribution makes a simple comparison unreliable.

text:
10. Check your understanding
A researcher compares the mean of 20 new learners with the published mean from 12 learners in an earlier study. They enter the earlier mean as mu in a one-sample t-test.
What uncertainty has been omitted?






Check your reasoning





The earlier mean is itself an estimate with sampling uncertainty. Treating it as a fixed population value ignores that uncertainty. title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
1. Your question
Our target is mean A minus mean B, in score points. A negative estimate means A has the lower mean; a positive estimate means A has the higher mean.
This example uses 40 synthetic learners, with 20 complete scores per group. The scores reuse the observed values from Chapter 03 for a standalone illustration. Excluding that chapter’s missing scores would require justification in an applied study.

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text: How much does the population mean assessment score differ between teaching approaches A and B?

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
2. When to use this method
Use an independent-samples t-test to compare the means of a numerical outcome in two independent groups.
Examples include yield from independently assigned field plots, expenditure among independent customers in two groups, and assessment scores from different learners.
Welch’s t-test estimates the difference without assuming equal population variances. It is a useful starting choice for independent mean comparisons. It still requires a suitable design and attention to the outcome distributions.



Design
Relevant approach




Different independent learners in A and B
Independent-samples t-test


Same learners before and after training
Paired t-test


Learners grouped within classrooms
A method accounting for classroom clustering


More than two independent groups
One-way ANOVA methods


Numerical outcome with important adjustment variables
Linear regression, with appropriate design and diagnostics



Equal group sizes do not make observations paired. Meaningful pairing must come from the design.

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests

Target: \(\mu_A-\mu_B\), the population mean difference.
Null hypothesis: \(H_0: \mu_A-\mu_B=0\).
Two-sided alternative: \(H_1: \mu_A-\mu_B\ne0\).

Welch’s estimated standard error is:
\[
SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_A^2}{n_A}+\frac{s_B^2}{n_B}}.
\]
The test statistic is:
\[
t = \frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{SE}.
\]
The confidence interval is the estimated difference plus or minus a t critical value multiplied by this SE. Welch’s method uses approximate degrees of freedom that can be fractional.






Optional: Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom





\[
\nu = \frac{(s_A^2/n_A+s_B^2/n_B)^2}
{(s_A^2/n_A)^2/(n_A-1)+(s_B^2/n_B)^2/(n_B-1)}.
\]
This accounts for uncertainty in the two variance estimates. Unlike the pooled equal-variance test, the degrees of freedom need not equal \(n_A+n_B-2\).

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
4. Check your data and assumptions
Before testing, verify:

Each learner contributes one score and belongs to one group.
Observations are independent within and between groups; classroom or household dependence is addressed.
Scores have consistent units and a meaningful numerical scale.
Missing scores, duplicate records, and exclusions have been investigated.
Group distributions do not show severe skewness or influential extremes that undermine small-sample inference.
Sampling and assignment support the population and interpretation of interest.

Inspect individual scores and Q-Q plots within each group. The group SDs are approximately 6.97 and 13.96 points, so equal variability should not be assumed. Welch’s method addresses unequal variances, but does not correct dependence, selection bias, or confounding.

Welch versus pooled Student’s t-test
The pooled test assumes equal population variances and uses a pooled variance estimate. Welch’s test allows unequal variances. Do not automatically select between them using a preliminary variance-test p-value. Choose an approach based on the design and a justified analysis plan.
A normality-test p-value alone should not decide whether to use a mean comparison or a rank-based method. They can address different inferential targets.

I want to compare assessment scores from two independent groups, with 20 learners per group. Define the difference as A minus B. Mean scores are 69.30 and 74.10; SDs are approximately 6.97 and 13.96. text:
8. Report your finding

In the synthetic example, mean scores were 69.30 points (SD 6.97, n=20) for A and 74.10 points (SD 13.96, n=20) for B. The estimated difference, A minus B, was -4.80 points (95% CI -11.95 to 2.35). A two-sided Welch t-test yielded \(t(27.91)=-1.38\), \(p=0.1798\). The interval includes zero and potentially important differences; these results do not establish equivalence. title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
9. Common mistakes and alternatives







Mistake
Better approach




Using a paired test because group sizes match
Identify whether observations are genuinely linked


Ignoring clustering within classrooms
Account for the correlated structure


Changing the comparison direction midway
State A minus B consistently in code and reporting


Assuming p > 0.05 means equality
Examine precision and important differences; use equivalence methods when appropriate


Inferring causation from a group comparison alone
Assess assignment, confounding, and the broader design


Searching for a test with a smaller p-value
Preserve the inferential target and document justified changes



Severe skewness, influential observations, or a different target quantity may motivate another approach. Mann–Whitney is a rank-based comparison and does not generally test arithmetic means or only medians. Transformations change the scale of inference. Regression may support adjustment for prespecified covariates, but adjustment alone does not establish causation. Review the relevant method’s assumptions before switching.

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
10. Check your understanding
An analyst reports a mean difference A minus B of -4.80 points, with a 95% interval from -11.95 to 2.35, then writes: “B is certainly better, but the test had no effect because p > 0.05.”
Which parts need correction?






Check your reasoning





B has the higher sample mean, but uncertainty includes zero and a small difference in the opposite direction. The interval also includes potentially important differences favoring B. A large p-value does not establish no effect. “Better” additionally requires a meaningful outcome, practical context, and a design that supports the intended claim.

title: Independent-Samples t-Test
text:
Next step

title: Paired t-Test
text:
1. Your question
The same 16 synthetic learners complete two assessments. Define each learner’s change as after minus before, in points. Positive changes mean higher scores after training.
The learner is the independent unit. Two scores from each learner form one pair; they are not two independent learners. These are new synthetic data for this chapter.

title: Paired t-Test
text: What is the population mean change in assessment score from before to after training?

title: Paired t-Test
text:
2. When to use this method
Use a paired t-test for two numerical measurements linked by a meaningful pairing, when the target is a population mean difference.








Example
Pairing unit
Difference




Assessment before and after training
Learner
After minus before


Two measurement devices used on each specimen
Specimen
Device A minus Device B


Matched treatment and comparison plots
Matched pair
Treated minus comparison



Distinct pairs must provide independent information. Matching must be justified by the design, not invented by sorting the outcomes. Matching does not by itself eliminate confounding.
Use an independent-samples method for different, unmatched units in two groups. More than two repeated conditions generally requires a repeated-measures approach.

title: Paired t-Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
Let \(d_i = \text{after}_i-\text{before}_i\), and let \(\mu_d\) denote the population mean change.

Null hypothesis: \(H_0: \mu_d=0\).
Two-sided alternative: \(H_1: \mu_d\ne0\).
Estimate: The sample mean change, \(\bar d\).

The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on the differences:
\[
t = \frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}, \qquad df=n-1.
\]
Here, \(n\) is the number of complete pairs and \(s_d\) is the sample SD of the differences. A 95% interval for the population mean change is:
\[
\bar d \pm t_{0.975,n-1}\frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
The SE uses variation in the paired differences. It does not come from treating the before and after scores as independent groups.

title: Paired t-Test
text:
4. Check the pairing and assumptions







Check
What to establish




Matching
Each before score is linked to the correct after score by an identifier


Independent pairs
Different learners are independent, with no unaccounted classroom or household clustering


Complete pairs
Both measurements are available for each included pair


Measurement consistency
Same meaningful scale, units, and comparable assessment procedures


Difference distribution
Inspect changes for strong skewness and influential extremes


Sampling and timing
Understand recruitment, assessment timing, and other changes between assessments



For exact small-sample t inference, the differences are assumed normally distributed. The before and after distributions do not each need to be normal. At 16 pairs, inspect the changes carefully rather than treating a normality-test result as a pass/fail rule.

Preserve identities
The supplied CSV has one row per learner and separate before and after columns. If the measurements come from separate files, verify unique IDs and perform a checked join. Audit unmatched records and duplicated keys. Never pair the files merely by row position or sort the two score columns separately.


Missing measurements
An incomplete pair cannot supply an observed within-pair change. Count incomplete pairs and investigate why measurements are missing before deciding how to handle them. Complete-pair analysis can be biased when the retained learners differ systematically from those with missing measurements.
The supplied script stops if scores are missing, allowing you to investigate. It does not silently omit incomplete pairs or impute scores.

7. Use AI and check its suggestions

I have before and after assessment scores for the same 16 learners, stored as one row per learner with a unique ID. Define change as after minus before. Explain a paired t-test and the relevant assumptions. Show how to check the matching and missing pairs, and verify the equivalent one-sample test on changes. Do not analyze the 32 scores as independent observations or conclude that training caused the change.

Check that the response:

Uses paired = TRUE with after listed first, or a one-sample test of after-minus-before differences.
Counts 16 pairs and uses 15 degrees of freedom.
Checks normality of differences rather than requiring both raw distributions to be normal.
Preserves ID matching and investigates missing pairs.
Separates evidence of mean change from evidence of a causal training effect.

title: Paired t-Test
text:
8. Report your finding

Among 16 synthetic learners with complete paired measurements, the mean score increased from 65.81 to 70.06 points. Mean within-learner change, defined as after minus before, was 4.25 points (SD of changes 4.36; 95% CI 1.93 to 6.57). A two-sided paired t-test yielded \(t(15)=3.90\), \(p=0.00142\). The results provide evidence of a positive mean change under the test assumptions. Without a suitable comparison design, the change cannot be attributed solely to training.

For an applied report, describe recruitment, timing, diagnostic findings, missing pairs, and relevant changes in assessment procedures or conditions.

Mistake

Treating 32 scores as independent observations

If differences are strongly skewed or contain influential extremes, first investigate data quality and the inferential target. A signed-rank test assumes a suitable symmetric difference distribution for a location interpretation and does not generally test the arithmetic mean. 10. Check your understanding
An AI tool sorts the before scores from smallest to largest, independently sorts the after scores, then performs a paired test.
Why is this invalid even if the mean change stays the same?






Check your reasoning





Separate sorting destroys the actual learner pairing. Although the difference of means remains the same for complete data, the constructed differences, their SD, the SE, confidence interval, and p-value can change. Restore the verified ID matching before calculating changes.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
1. Your question
We observe eight synthetic participants in each group. Each participant completes the task once. Lower completion times mean faster completion.
The example emphasizes ordering rather than a difference in arithmetic means. It is a new dataset, separate from the assessment scores in previous chapters.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text: Do task completion times tend to be higher in one of two independent groups?

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
2. When to use this method
The Mann–Whitney U test, also called the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, uses the pooled ranks of numerical or ordered outcomes from two independent groups.
It can be useful when ordering is meaningful and the question concerns relative tendency rather than a specific arithmetic mean difference. It does not require normal outcome distributions, but it still requires a suitable sampling design and independent observations.



Question or design
Consider




Rank-based comparison of two independent groups
Mann–Whitney U test


Difference in independent population means
Welch’s t-test


Paired numerical or ordered observations
Wilcoxon signed-rank method, with its own conditions


Several independent groups
Kruskal–Wallis test



Do not choose this test solely because a normality test gives a small p-value. First identify the quantity or comparison you want to explain.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
For the standard test in this chapter, the null hypothesis is that the two populations have the same outcome distribution. Under that null, group labels are exchangeable for the rank calculation. The two-sided procedure detects departures that produce sufficiently unusual rank sums; it is not equally sensitive to every possible difference between distributions.
A useful accompanying effect estimate is:
\[
\theta = P(X_A > X_B) + \tfrac12 P(X_A = X_B).
\]
This describes the probability that a randomly selected A outcome exceeds an independently selected B outcome, with half credit for ties. The sample estimate compares every observed A value with every observed B value.
For completion times, a value below 0.5 means A tends to have shorter, not longer, times in this pairwise sense. This is not a within-person improvement probability or evidence of causation.






Not automatically a test of medians



If distributions differ only by a location shift and otherwise have the same shape and spread, a location interpretation is reasonable and a shift also corresponds to a difference in medians. Without those additional conditions, rejection should not automatically be described as evidence of different medians.
The usual null-calibrated Mann–Whitney test is also not a generally valid test of only \(\theta=0.5\) under arbitrary unequal distributions. Methods designed for that weaker null require separate consideration.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
4. Check your data and assumptions

Verify that observations are independent within and between groups.
Confirm that the outcome has a meaningful order and is measured comparably.
Check missing values, group labels, duplicate IDs, and unexpected measurements.
Inspect individual observations and empirical cumulative distribution curves.
Identify ties, which affect the rank calculation and available p-value methods.
Assess shape and spread before making a location or median interpretation.

A rank transformation does not remove clustering, confounding, or missing-data bias. Valid extreme observations still matter through their ordering; ranks do not justify ignoring data-quality checks.

Exact and approximate p-values
This small example has no ties, so we request an exact two-sided p-value. The exact null distribution comes from possible allocations of the pooled ranks to groups of the observed sizes.
For larger samples or tied values, software may use a tie-adjusted normal approximation, possibly with a continuity correction, or a supported permutation procedure. Record the method and settings. Do not ignore software warnings or assume all implementations use the same defaults.
The supplied script stops if ties are introduced because its documented example specifically uses the untied exact calculation. This is a teaching guard, not a claim that tied outcomes cannot be analyzed.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
8. Report your finding

In this synthetic example, completion times had medians of 24.5 minutes in A and 41.5 minutes in B, with eight independent participants per group. A two-sided exact Mann–Whitney test yielded \(U_A=17\) and \(p=0.1304\). The estimated probability of an A time exceeding a B time was 0.266, indicating a sample tendency toward shorter times in A. The small sample provides limited evidence against equal distributions; the result does not establish equivalence, a median-specific difference, or a causal group effect.

title: Mann–Whitney U Test
text:
10. Check your understanding
Two groups have the same median but different spreads. An AI response says a Mann–Whitney test must give a large p-value because the medians match.
Is that reasoning sufficient?






Check your reasoning





No. Equal medians do not imply identical distributions or determine a rank-sum p-value. The result depends on the full observed ordering and the sampling distribution of the statistic. Conversely, the rank-sum test is not guaranteed to detect every spread difference. Inspect the distributions and state the inferential target before interpreting the result.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
1. Your question
Ten synthetic learners have before and after scores. Define change as after minus before. Positive values indicate higher scores after training.
This new dataset illustrates a small exact signed-rank calculation. It is separate from Chapter 06’s paired t-test example; do not compare their p-values as if they came from the same observations.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text: Are paired assessment-score changes centered around zero under a suitable symmetric location model?

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
2. When to use this method
The Wilcoxon signed-rank test uses the signs and ranks of the absolute paired differences. It can support inference about a symmetric location of paired numerical differences without requiring a normal distribution.
The differences and their absolute magnitudes must be meaningful. Arbitrary numerical codes for ordered categories may not provide a defensible scale for this calculation.



Question or design
Consider




Location of paired numerical differences, with plausible symmetry
Signed-rank test


Population mean paired difference
Paired t-test, when suitable


Direction of paired differences without a symmetry assumption
A suitable sign test


Independent groups
Mann–Whitney U test, with its own target and assumptions



Do not automatically substitute signed ranks for a paired t-test after a normality test rejects. First consider the target quantity, symmetry, and design.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
For the standard signed-rank test, the null model assumes independent differences from a continuous distribution symmetric about zero. The two-sided test assesses departures from that zero center within an appropriate symmetric location framework.
Symmetry means the distribution has a similar shape on either side of its center. A symmetric distribution need not be normal.
A related location estimate is the pseudomedian, estimated by the median of the Walsh averages:
\[
\frac{d_i+d_j}{2}, \qquad i\leq j.
\]
Under symmetry, the population pseudomedian equals the distribution’s center and median. In general, it need not equal the population median, and its sample estimate need not equal the sample median of changes.






State the assumptions with the interpretation



The signed-rank test is not generally a test of only “median change equals zero” for arbitrary asymmetric distributions. It also does not directly test the arithmetic mean change. If symmetry is implausible, reconsider the inferential target and method.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
4. Check before running

Verify each pair using a unique identifier.
Confirm that different pairs supply independent information.
Investigate missing measurements and report incomplete pairs.
Inspect the differences for skewness, asymmetry, and unusual values.
Count zero differences and repeated absolute differences.
Check that subtraction and magnitude comparisons are meaningful on the outcome scale.

A small sample provides limited evidence about symmetry. Subject knowledge and the measurement process matter alongside plots. A plot cannot establish independence or rule out missing-data bias.

Zeros and tied absolute differences
Zero differences have no positive or negative sign. In the usual Wilcoxon convention, zero differences are omitted before ranking; other conventions, such as Pratt’s, handle them differently.
Tied absolute differences receive average ranks. Their presence changes the null distribution and p-value calculation. Software may use an approximation or a supported conditional/permutation method. Document the software, zero convention, ties, and exact or approximate calculation.
This example has no zeros or tied absolute differences. The supplied script stops if these occur, preserving this specific exact teaching calculation. That guard does not imply such data are unanalyzable.

10. Check your understanding
A report says: “The rank-biserial effect was 0.8545, so 85.45% of learners improved.”
What is wrong?






Check your reasoning





The effect is a standardized balance of positive and negative rank sums. It is not a proportion of learners. In this example, eight of ten learners, or 80%, had positive changes. Neither number is a causal improvement estimate.

title: One-Way ANOVA
text:
1. Your question
This example contains 24 synthetic learners, eight per approach. Each contributes one numerical score. We assume independently observed learners for illustration; real classroom clustering would require a different analysis.
The overall question concerns equality of population means. Follow-up questions concern specific differences such as A minus C, expressed in score points.

title: One-Way ANOVA
text: Do population mean assessment scores differ among teaching approaches A, B, and C?

title: One-Way ANOVA
text:
2. When to use this method
One-way ANOVA compares a numerical outcome across levels of one categorical grouping variable. “One-way” refers to one grouping factor, not to a one-sided alternative.



Design or target
Starting method




Several independent population means, unequal variances allowed
Welch’s one-way ANOVA


Several independent means with a defensible common variance
Classical one-way ANOVA


Same units measured under several conditions
Repeated-measures methods


Several predictors or adjustment variables
An appropriate regression model


Rank-based comparison across independent groups
Kruskal–Wallis, with a different inferential target



Welch’s ANOVA is the primary method in this example. Classical ANOVA is included to explain the variance decomposition and its additional common-variance assumption. Do not select the method that produces the smaller p-value.

title: One-Way ANOVA
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
For three groups:

Null: \(H_0: \mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C\).
Alternative: At least one population mean differs.

A small overall p-value does not identify which groups differ, establish that all pairs differ, or measure practical importance.

Classical ANOVA
Classical ANOVA compares variation among group means with variation within groups:
\[
F=\frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{within}}}.
\]
With \(k\) groups and \(N\) independent observations, its degrees of freedom are \(k-1\) and \(N-k\). Under independent normal errors with a common variance, this ratio has an F distribution under the null.


Welch’s ANOVA
Welch’s method uses group-specific variance estimates to weight the means and adjusts the F statistic and degrees of freedom. Its denominator degrees of freedom may be fractional. It does not assume equal population variances, but still depends on suitable independence and distributional conditions.
An overall test answers whether the equal-means null is compatible with the evidence under its assumptions. Group means and pairwise difference estimates explain magnitude and direction.

title: One-Way ANOVA
text:
4. Check before running
Check independent units, consistent measurement, group labels, missing values, influential observations, and distributions within each group. Examine group sample sizes and spreads, especially when unequal variances coincide with unequal sample sizes.
Classical ANOVA additionally assumes a common error variance. Normality concerns errors within groups, not the pooled raw outcome distribution. Welch’s method accommodates unequal variances but can still be affected by severe skewness, heavy tails, or small groups.
A variance test or normality-test p-value should not automatically determine the analysis. Use design knowledge, plots, and method-specific reasoning. Equal group sizes do not establish equal population variances.
The diagnostic script shows raw group scores, residuals versus fitted group means, and a pooled residual Q-Q plot from the group-means model. The pooled Q-Q plot is only a summary: unequal group variances can affect its shape, so inspect the groups as well. These plots cannot establish independence or causal identification.

Decide the comparison family before inspecting which differences look promising. Here, the family is all three two-sided pairwise comparisons.

1. Your question
This synthetic example has eight independent participants per group, with one completion time per person. Lower values indicate faster completion. Groups A and B reuse the teaching values from Chapter 07; group C adds a third comparison group.

title: Kruskal–Wallis Test
text: Do task completion times differ in their rank-based tendency across groups A, B, and C?

title: Kruskal–Wallis Test
text:
2. When to use this method
The Kruskal–Wallis test compares pooled ranks across independent groups. It accommodates numerical or ordered outcomes without assuming normal distributions.
Use it when the outcome ordering is meaningful, units are independent, and its rank-based question fits the goal. It is not an automatic remedy for every violation of ANOVA assumptions.



Situation
Consider

title: Kruskal–Wallis Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
The usual null hypothesis is that all groups share the same outcome distribution. Under this null, group labels are exchangeable for the pooled-rank calculation.
The statistic measures differences among group mean ranks. A sufficiently large value provides evidence against the common-distribution null, but the test is not equally sensitive to every possible distributional departure.
For \(k\) groups with sample sizes \(n_j\), pooled rank sums \(R_j\), and total sample size \(N\), the uncorrected statistic is:
\[
H=\frac{12}{N(N+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\frac{R_j^2}{n_j}-3(N+1).
\]
With adequate sample sizes under the null, the statistic has an approximate chi-square distribution with \(k-1\) degrees of freedom. This is an approximation, not an exact p-value.






Not automatically a test of medians



If group distributions have the same shape and spread and differ only by location, a location interpretation is reasonable. Without those conditions, do not label a significant result as proof of different population medians.
Different group spreads can complicate interpretation. Rank-based does not mean assumption-free or universally robust to unequal variances.

title: Kruskal–Wallis Test
text:
4. Check before running
Verify independent units, comparable measurements, group labels, missingness, duplicate IDs, and meaningful outcome ordering. Inspect individual values and empirical cumulative distribution curves to understand shape, spread, and overlap.
Ties receive average pooled ranks. The usual statistic is divided by the tie correction:
\[
C=1-\frac{\sum_l(t_l^3-t_l)}{N^3-N},
\]
where \(t_l\) is the size of each tied-value block. With no ties, \(C=1\). If all values are identical, \(C=0\) and the usual statistic is undefined.
Very small groups, sparse ordered categories, or many ties can make the chi-square approximation unreliable. Consider a suitable exact or permutation implementation when needed, preserving any design restrictions. Permuting labels is only justified when the null and sampling or assignment mechanism support exchangeability.
The example has eight observations per group and no ties. We use the conventional chi-square approximation and clearly label it. A sample-size rule alone cannot guarantee accuracy.

title: Repeated-Measures ANOVA and Friedman Test
text:
3. What repeated-measures ANOVA tests
For three assessment occasions:

Null: The three population condition means are equal.
Alternative: At least one condition mean differs.

The analysis separates stable differences between learners from condition variation and within-learner error. The overall test does not identify specific differing occasions.

Sphericity
For the usual univariate repeated-measures F test with more than two conditions, sphericity requires equal variances of all pairwise difference scores. It is not the same as equal raw score variances at each occasion.
When sphericity fails, the uncorrected F test can have an inflated Type I error rate. Greenhouse–Geisser correction multiplies both degrees of freedom by an estimated epsilon while leaving the F statistic unchanged. The p-value is then recalculated with the corrected degrees of freedom.
The script reports both uncorrected and corrected results and treats the corrected result as primary. It does not implement Mauchly’s test or use a preliminary sphericity-test p-value to select the reported result. Correction does not repair independence violations, outliers, biased sampling, or an unsuitable mean model.
crumbs: 11  Repeated-Measures ANOVA and Friedman Test

title: Repeated-Measures ANOVA and Friedman Test
text:
4. What Friedman tests
Friedman ranks the conditions within each learner, then compares condition rank sums across learners. Its usual null calibration assumes that within-block condition labels are exchangeable under the null, with independent blocks. A randomized block design can justify exchangeability; in observational repeated-time data, the null assumptions require care.
The test detects systematic condition differences in within-block ranks. It does not directly test population mean equality and is not automatically a test of equal marginal medians. A location interpretation needs additional model conditions.
Ties within a learner receive average ranks, and the statistic is tie-corrected. Base R’s conventional p-value uses a chi-square approximation with k minus 1 degrees of freedom. With few blocks or many ties, consider whether a suitable exact or restricted permutation calculation is needed.






A rank test still needs the correct design



Friedman does not remove dependence between learners, account for arbitrary serial covariance, or make time points exchangeable by itself. It also does not establish a causal effect of training.

Missing visits require an explicit strategy. Removing every learner with any missing visit can alter the population represented and introduce bias. The supplied script stops for missing values instead of silently excluding learners. A mixed model may use incomplete records under specified assumptions, but is not automatically immune to missing-data bias.

2. When to use this method
Pearson’s chi-square test of independence assesses association between two categorical variables using cell counts from independent units and an appropriate sampling design.



Situation
Consider




Association in an adequately populated contingency table
Chi-square test of independence


Sparse table, particularly a small two-by-two table

The same Pearson statistic can test homogeneity of category proportions across independently sampled groups. Explain the actual sampling design; it determines which margins are fixed by design and how broadly the result can be generalized.
Do not enter percentages as if they were counts, or ordinary survey weights as if they represented independent people. Multiple-response questions also require care because one person may otherwise be counted in several cells.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence
text:
3. What it tests

Null hypothesis: Experience and learning preference are independent in the population.
Alternative: The variables are associated.

Under independence, each expected count is:
\[
E_{ij}=\frac{(\text{row total}_i)(\text{column total}_j)}{N}.
\]
Pearson’s statistic is:
\[
X^2=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}},
\]
where \(O_{ij}\) is the observed count. Under suitable conditions, the statistic has an approximate chi-square distribution with \((r-1)(c-1)\) degrees of freedom.
This is an overall association test. It does not directly identify causal effects or supply a separate adjusted test for every cell.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence
text:
4. Check counts, categories, and assumptions
Verify that units are independent, categories are mutually exclusive and consistently coded, and counts are nonnegative integers. Investigate missing responses and exclusions. Confirm whether the table represents raw counts or weighted estimates.
Inspect expected counts, not only observed counts, when assessing the approximation. A common diagnostic convention is that no expected count is below 1 and at least 80% are at least 5. This is a guideline rather than a universal guarantee; table structure and the sampling model matter.
In this example, the smallest expected count is 15, so sparse expected cells are not a concern. Independence and sampling quality still require design evidence.
A zero observed count is not automatically a problem if its expected count is adequate. A structural zero, representing an impossible category combination, changes the model and may invalidate the usual degrees-of-freedom calculation. Entirely empty rows or columns also need investigation.
For a two-by-two table, some software applies Yates’s continuity correction by default. This example is two-by-three and explicitly sets correct = FALSE for a consistent uncorrected Pearson calculation.

2. When to use this method
Fisher’s exact test is useful for independent contingency tables, particularly small two-by-two tables where chi-square approximations may be questionable. It can also be used with larger counts; it is not restricted to small samples.



Situation

Exact inference does not remove the need for independent units, appropriate sampling, or correct category definitions. Complex survey weights, repeated responses, and clustering require appropriate methods.

title: Fisher’s Exact Test
text:
3. What it tests
In the two-by-two setting, the null hypothesis is that the population odds ratio equals one: no association between row and column categories under the sampling model.
Fisher’s test conditions on the observed row and column totals. Under the null, the top-left cell follows a hypergeometric distribution. The calculation considers tables with these same margins.
The usual two-sided definition used by R sums the null probabilities of tables whose probabilities are no greater than that of the observed table, allowing for numerical tolerance. A two-sided p-value is not always twice the smaller one-sided p-value. State the software and definition when comparing implementations.
“Exact” refers to calibration using the conditional null distribution rather than a large-sample approximation. It does not mean the interpretation is certain or that the effect is precisely estimated. Because counts are discrete, achievable p-values are also discrete and tests can be conservative.

title: Fisher’s Exact Test
text:
4. Check before running
Verify that:

Each participant contributes to one cell only.
Counts are nonnegative integers, not percentages or ordinary survey weights.
Rows and columns represent clearly defined, mutually exclusive categories.
Missing outcomes and exclusions are investigated.
Sampling or assignment supports the conditional analysis and intended generalization.
Structural zeros, impossible combinations, and empty margins are addressed.

Expected counts here are 4.5 completed and 5.5 not completed in each row. The small expected counts motivate examining an exact approach rather than relying only on a chi-square approximation.
A zero observed cell does not prevent Fisher’s test when margins are valid, but odds-ratio estimates or interval limits may be zero or infinite. Do not add an arbitrary constant to all cells merely to make software output finite; any correction changes the estimation procedure and needs justification.

Verify the p-value
The observed table’s null probability is:
\[
P(A_{11}=8)=\frac{\binom{9}{8}\binom{11}{2}}{\binom{20}{10}}.
\]
For these symmetric row totals, tables with top-left counts 0, 1, 8, and 9 have probabilities no greater than the observed table’s. Summing their probabilities gives approximately 0.0054775.
This provides evidence against the no-association null under the conditional model. It is not the probability that the null is true or that the difference was caused by chance.


Distinguish the odds-ratio estimates
The completion odds are 8/2 in A and 1/9 in B, giving:
\[
\widehat{OR}_{\text{cross-product}}=\frac{8/2}{1/9}=36.
\]
Base R’s fisher.test() instead reports the conditional maximum-likelihood estimate, approximately 27.33, based on the conditional model. The two estimates need not agree in small samples. Report which estimate you use and pair it with an interval from the stated procedure.
The conditional interval is very wide despite the small p-value. The evidence against OR=1 does not mean we know the association magnitude precisely.


Odds are not probabilities
The sample completion proportion ratio is 0.80/0.10=8, while the cross-product odds ratio is 36. An odds ratio of 36 does not mean participants are 36 times as likely to complete. Which probability measures are estimable also depends on sampling design; case-control samples do not directly estimate population risks from sampled row proportions without additional information.
Reversing one dimension of the table reciprocates the odds ratio. Reversing both dimensions restores it. The two-sided association p-value is unchanged by such relabeling, but interpretation still requires correct labels.

text:
3. Define the outcome and denominator
State what counts as completion, the assessment window, and who belongs in the denominator. Missing or pending outcomes should not silently become failures or disappear from the denominator.
Do not compare percentages without their sample sizes. A proportion of 70% from seven of ten people has different precision from 700 of 1000.
The input CSV stores completed counts and totals. total is the denominator, not the number who did not complete. Check that completed counts are integers between zero and total.

title: Tests for Proportions
section: 4. What the tests estimate or test
text:
4. What the tests estimate or test

One proportion
Let \(p_A\) be the population completion probability in A.

Null: \(p_A=0.50\).
Two-sided alternative: \(p_A\ne0.50\).
Estimate: \(\hat p_A=42/60=0.70\).

We use an exact binomial test and a Clopper–Pearson exact interval. The interval has at least nominal coverage under the binomial model and can be conservative because outcomes are discrete.
The two-sided exact p-value sums null probabilities of outcomes no more probable than the observed outcome under the specified procedure. It is not always twice a one-sided p-value, and the equal-tailed interval need not be the exact inversion of every two-sided p-value definition.


Two independent proportions

Null: \(p_A-p_B=0\).
Two-sided alternative: \(p_A-p_B\ne0\).
Estimate: \(0.70-0.50=0.20\), or 20 percentage points.

For the uncorrected large-sample equal-proportions test, the pooled estimate under the null is \(\hat p=(42+30)/(60+60)=0.60\):
\[
z=\frac{\hat p_A-\hat p_B}
{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_A+1/n_B)}}.
\]
R reports the equivalent chi-square statistic \(X^2=z^2\) with one degree of freedom.

title: Tests for Proportions
text:
5. Check before running
Verify independent participants within and between groups, consistent outcome definitions, complete denominators, missingness, and the sampling process. A fixed reference must be chosen for substantive reasons; a reference estimated from another sample carries uncertainty.
For a normal-approximation test, check expected event and non-event counts under the null. Here they are 36 and 24 in each group, so sparsity is not a concern. Approximate intervals can still perform poorly near zero or one or with small samples.
For interval estimation, score-based methods for single proportions and Newcombe or other suitable methods for differences may offer better coverage than a simple Wald interval. This base R example explicitly labels the two-sample interval it uses instead of presenting it as exact.

text:
2. When to use this method
McNemar’s test compares the marginal probabilities of a binary outcome in paired measurements. Examples include before-and-after task completion or two binary diagnostic classifications on the same specimens.



Design or question
Consider




Two paired binary outcomes
McNemar’s test


Independent binary groups
Tests for proportions or Fisher’s exact test


Paired categorical outcome with more than two categories
A suitable marginal-homogeneity generalization


More than two repeated binary measurements
Cochran’s Q under suitable conditions, or an appropriate repeated-outcome model


Adjustment variables or clustering between participants
A suitable paired or longitudinal binary-outcome model



Do not apply an ordinary independence test to the before-by-after transition table when the question is marginal change. Independence of before and after is a different null from equality of their marginal Yes probabilities.

title: McNemar’s Test
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
Let \(p_{NY}\) denote the population probability of No before and Yes after, and \(p_{YN}\) the reverse.

Null: \(p_{NY}=p_{YN}\), equivalent to equal marginal Yes probabilities.
Two-sided alternative: The transition probabilities differ.
Effect estimate: The after-minus-before Yes proportion difference.

For complete pairs:
\[
\widehat\Delta=\hat p_{\text{after}}-\hat p_{\text{before}}
=\frac{\text{gains}-\text{losses}}{n}.
\]
The concordant pairs remain relevant to the marginal proportions and their denominator, but they do not distinguish gains from losses in the conditional test.

Exact conditional test
Condition on the number of discordant pairs, \(m\). Under the null, gains follow a binomial distribution with \(m\) trials and probability 0.5. We use a two-sided exact binomial test as the primary procedure.


Approximate McNemar test
With sufficient discordant information, the uncorrected statistic is:
\[
X^2=\frac{(\text{gains}-\text{losses})^2}{\text{gains}+\text{losses}},
\]
compared with a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom. A continuity-corrected version reduces the numerator’s absolute difference by one before squaring in this example. Exact and approximate p-values need not match.

title: McNemar’s Test
text:
4. Check the pairs and input
Verify matching identifiers in the underlying records, consistent outcome definitions, complete paired assessments, and independence between participants. Several participants from the same household or classroom may require additional dependence handling.
The supplied CSV contains four aggregated transition counts. It cannot verify matching or reveal whether missing visits were excluded. An applied workflow should audit individual records before aggregation.
Use actual counts, not percentages. Confirm row and column direction and ensure categories are identical at both occasions. Investigate incomplete pairs; simply dropping them can bias the comparison if missingness relates to outcome or change.
The amount of discordant information matters more to the conditional test than the total sample alone. Here, 22 pairs are discordant. We use the exact conditional method without selecting a procedure according to which gives the smallest p-value.
If there are no discordant pairs, there is no observed directional change to test conditionally. The supplied script stops for this case. Report the lack of discordance without claiming that population change is proven absent; estimation and uncertainty still require care.

# Primary exact conditional test among discordant pairs.

A paired risk-difference interval requires a method that uses the matched structure; subtracting separate independent-proportion interval limits is not a substitute. This introductory example reports the marginal difference as a point estimate and leaves its interval for a dedicated matched-proportion estimation extension.


Read the plot
The transition figure shows four mutually exclusive participant groups. Compare the two colored discordant bars to understand the test’s directional evidence. The unchanged groups contribute to the total population represented, even though they do not enter the conditional binomial test.

8. Report your finding

In 60 complete synthetic paired observations, task completion increased from 22/60 (36.7%) before to 36/60 (60.0%) after assessment, a descriptive increase of 23.3 percentage points. Eighteen participants changed from No to Yes and four from Yes to No. A two-sided exact conditional McNemar procedure gave p=0.00434. No interval for the paired marginal difference is supplied here, and the comparison does not establish a causal training effect.
