title: Pearson Correlation
text:
1. Your question
The synthetic dataset contains 16 independent learners. Each row links one learner’s study hours during the preceding week with their assessment score. These two measurements must remain together.
The target is the population Pearson correlation, written \(\rho\). We estimate it using the sample correlation, \(r\).

title: Pearson Correlation
text: How strongly are study hours and assessment scores linearly associated among learners?

title: Pearson Correlation
text:
2. When to use this method
Pearson correlation summarizes the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two numerical variables with nonzero variation.



Goal or design
Consider




Linear association between two numerical variables
Pearson correlation


Monotonic association using ranks
Spearman correlation


Change in outcome units per predictor unit
Linear regression


Repeated observations within participants
A method accounting for within-participant dependence


Agreement between two measurement methods
An agreement analysis; correlation alone is insufficient



Computing a descriptive correlation does not require normally distributed data. The usual t-test and Fisher-transformed interval rely on additional inferential assumptions discussed below.

title: Pearson Correlation
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
The sample correlation is:
\[
r=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}}.
\]
It ranges from -1 to +1. Positive values indicate that larger x values tend to accompany larger y values along a linear pattern; negative values indicate the reverse. Values near zero indicate weak linear association, but can coexist with a strong curved relationship.
Correlation is unitless and symmetric: swapping x and y leaves r unchanged. Changing hours to minutes also leaves it unchanged. Multiplying one variable by a negative constant reverses its sign.
For this two-sided test:

Null: \(H_0: \rho=0\).
Alternative: \(H_1: \rho\ne0\).

Under independent observations from a bivariate normal population, the statistic
\[
t=r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}
\]
has a t distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom under the null. Zero correlation is not generally equivalent to independence outside special models such as joint normality.

title: Pearson Correlation
text:
4. Check before running

Keep the measurements aligned
A pair here means two variables measured on the same learner. That does not make the analysis a paired t-test: correlation examines association, whereas a paired t-test examines a mean difference on a meaningful common scale.
Check unique IDs, missing values, units, ranges, and row alignment. Never sort the two columns independently. If excluding incomplete records, document the number and reasons and consider possible missing-data bias.


Inspect the scatterplot
Look for a roughly linear pattern, influential points, clusters, restricted ranges, and changes in spread. Separate groups can create a pooled correlation that differs substantially from within-group associations. Time trends can also produce misleading associations when observations are dependent.
Pearson’s r can be strongly affected by one influential observation. Verify unusual values against source records; do not delete valid observations just to strengthen the correlation.


Separate description from inference
The standard test assumes independent paired observations and a suitable joint distribution; bivariate normality is a standard sufficient condition for its exact null t calibration. Separate marginal normality checks do not establish joint normality.
The usual Fisher-z interval is approximate. With small samples, influential observations, or substantial nonnormality, its coverage and the test’s calibration may be unreliable. A suitable bootstrap or other robust procedure needs assumptions matched to the sampling design; it is not an automatic repair.

                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fit <- cor.test(dat$study_hours, dat$score, method = "pearson",
                alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
print(fit)
Inspect the relationship before interpreting the number:
plot(dat$study_hours, dat$score,
     xlab = "Study time (hours in preceding week)",

abline(lm(score ~ study_hours, data = dat))

Check that df equals \(16-2=14\) and substitute r into the test-statistic formula. Swapping the variables should give the same r, p-value, and interval.
The sample shows a pronounced positive linear association. The interval estimates uncertainty about population correlation under the inferential model. It is not an interval containing 95% of score observations or predicted scores.

How the interval is constructed
R’s usual Pearson interval transforms the correlation using Fisher’s z:
\[
z_r=\operatorname{atanh}(r),\qquad SE(z_r)\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-3}}.
\]
Calculate an approximate normal interval on that scale and transform its limits back using the hyperbolic tangent. This keeps the interval within the correlation range. It does not make the interval exact.


Sensitivity checks
The script calculates r after omitting each learner in turn. Inspect whether a single omission changes the interpretation substantially. This is a diagnostic aid, not permission to select the omission producing the preferred result. Report consequential sensitivity and investigate the underlying observation.


Correlation is not a slope, agreement, or causation
An r of 0.912 does not mean each additional hour adds 0.912 score points. A regression slope answers that units-based question.
Two devices can correlate almost perfectly while one consistently reads ten units higher; correlation does not establish agreement.
The association between study hours and scores could reflect prior ability, motivation, access to resources, or other factors. A small p-value does not establish that increasing study hours causes higher scores.
In simple ordinary least-squares regression with an intercept using these same complete observations, \(r^2\) equals the model’s sample R-squared. This special identity does not establish a causal percentage explained and should not be generalized to arbitrary models.

title: Spearman Correlation
text:
1. Your question
Twelve independent synthetic learners each contribute a practice-session count and a score. Two learners report two sessions, and two report four sessions. These repeated values are ties, not duplicate participants.
The target is a rank-based association between practice and score. It is not a score increase per session or a causal effect of practice.

title: Spearman Correlation
text: Do learners with more practice sessions tend to have higher assessment scores?

title: Spearman Correlation
text:
2. When to use this method
Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation calculated on the ranks of two variables. It describes monotonic association: as one variable increases, the other tends consistently upward or downward, without requiring a straight-line relationship on the original scale.



Question
Consider




Monotonic association for numerical or ordered variables
Spearman correlation


Linear association on original numerical scales
Pearson correlation


Outcome change in units per predictor unit
Linear regression, with an appropriate model


Agreement between measurements
An agreement method, not correlation alone



Monotonic does not mean every observation must follow the same ordering. Sampling variation and measurement noise can produce reversals.
Spearman can miss strong nonmonotonic relationships, such as a U-shaped pattern. It does not automatically solve clustering, confounding, missing-data bias, or influential observations.

title: Spearman Correlation
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
The sample coefficient is:
\[
r_s=\operatorname{cor}(\operatorname{rank}(X),\operatorname{rank}(Y)).
\]
Assign average ranks to tied values. The coefficient ranges from -1 to +1 when both rank vectors have nonzero variation. It is unitless and unchanged when the variables are swapped.
For continuous variables, population Spearman correlation can be defined as the correlation between their population cumulative-distribution transforms. With discrete or ordered variables, tie conventions matter to the corresponding rank-based target.
The conventional two-sided test is described as testing zero population Spearman correlation against a nonzero value. Its p-value calibration requires suitable independent observations and distributional or null assumptions. Exact permutation calibration is justified under an independence/exchangeability null; zero rank correlation alone is not equivalent to independence and does not justify arbitrary permutation under every dependent distribution.

A shortcut with limits
Without ties, the familiar identity is:
\[
r_s=1-\frac{6\sum_i d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)},
\]
where \(d_i\) is the difference between each observation’s two ranks. Do not apply this shortcut unchanged to tied data. Compute Pearson correlation of the average ranks instead.

title: Spearman Correlation
text:
4. Check before running
Verify IDs and row alignment, meaningful ordering, missing values, and nonconstant variables. Never independently sort the two columns. A learner’s practice count must remain linked to that learner’s score.
Inspect a scatterplot on the original scales. Look for monotonic patterns, subgroups, ceiling effects, restricted ranges, and influential observations. A rank plot can help reveal how the coefficient arises, but it does not replace the original-scale plot.
Rank-based measures require meaningful order, not equal intervals between ordinal categories. Code category order explicitly and justify it. For example, alphabetical ordering of Low, Medium, High would give the wrong ranks.
Many ties reduce the available ordering information and can affect attainable correlations and inference. Constant variables make the coefficient undefined. Missing values require an explicit strategy; complete-pair deletion can bias the analysis when missingness is informative.

                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
fit <- cor.test(dat$practice_sessions, dat$score, method = "spearman",
                alternative = "two.sided", exact = FALSE, continuity = FALSE)
print(fit)
Verify the coefficient directly:

score_rank <- rank(dat$score, ties.method = "average")
cor(practice_rank, score_rank, method = "pearson")

P-value settings
We explicitly use exact = FALSE and continuity = FALSE because this example has ties and uses R’s asymptotic t approximation. The coefficient is calculated from ranks; the small p-value is an approximation, not an exact permutation result.
At n=12, approximation quality needs caution even when the numerical result looks decisive. For a small applied study, consider a suitable permutation calculation under a defensible independence null. Preserve pairs while permuting one variable relative to the other, and respect any sampling or design restrictions. Report simulation settings and uncertainty if the permutation distribution is sampled rather than fully enumerated.

Confidence intervals
Base R’s cor.test() does not provide a Spearman confidence interval in this example. Do not copy a Pearson Fisher-z interval and label it as a Spearman interval without justification.
A suitable paired-observation bootstrap can estimate uncertainty under independent sampling, but small samples, ties, and degenerate resamples complicate coverage. This introductory script does not implement an interval. Report that limitation rather than inventing precision from the p-value.

title: Linear Regression
text:
1. Your question
This example reuses Chapter 16’s 16 synthetic learners, with a separate chapter-specific input file. Each row contains one independent learner’s study hours and score.
Pearson correlation summarized the linear association without units. Regression estimates a slope in score points per study hour. We begin with one predictor, then explain how adjustment changes interpretation.

title: Linear Regression
text: How does the mean assessment score relate to study hours during the preceding week?

title: Linear Regression
text:
2. When to use this method
Linear regression models a numerical outcome’s conditional mean as a function of one or more predictors. Predictors can be numerical or categorical when coded appropriately.
Use it for a units-based association or prediction question when the mean structure and error assumptions are defensible. Repeated observations, clustering, binary outcomes, and time dependence generally need a suitable extension or another model.
A bounded score is numerical, but linear predictions can extend outside its permitted range. Assess whether the model is appropriate within the range used, especially near boundaries.

title: Linear Regression
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
For one predictor:
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]
The model assumes the conditional mean is \(E(Y\mid X)=\beta_0+\beta_1X\), with errors having mean zero conditional on X.

Intercept, \(\beta_0\): Expected score at zero study hours, if that value is meaningful and the model applies there.
Slope, \(\beta_1\): Difference in expected score associated with one additional study hour.
Slope null: \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) in the specified model.

Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals. A residual is observed score minus fitted score.
The slope is an association parameter. Calling it an effect requires additional causal assumptions and design support.

title: Linear Regression
text:
4. Check before running







Condition
What to inspect




Independent errors
Sampling, clustering, repeated visits, and time ordering


Appropriate mean structure
Scatterplot, residual patterns, possible curves and interactions


Consistent measurement
Units, missingness, ranges, and row matching


Constant error variance for conventional SEs
Residual spread across fitted values


Error distribution for exact small-sample t inference
Residual Q-Q plot and influential observations


Identifiable predictors
No exact linear redundancy; inspect strong collinearity in larger models



Predictors do not need to be normally distributed. Normal-error assumptions concern the conditional outcome errors, not the marginal distribution of X. Residual checks provide imperfect evidence, especially with small samples.
Heteroscedasticity-robust SEs may support inference under suitable conditions when variance is not constant, but they do not correct a wrong mean structure, dependence, or confounding. They are not implemented in this base R example.

Influence is not an exclusion rule
Leverage identifies unusual predictor configurations. Residuals describe discrepancies from fitted values. Cook’s distance summarizes influence on the fitted coefficients. Investigate unusual cases and report meaningful sensitivity analyses; never automatically remove valid observations to improve model fit or significance.

R-squared
The sample R-squared of about 0.832 means the fitted line accounts for about 83.2% of the observed score sum-of-squares variation around the sample mean. It does not establish that study time causes 83.2% of score variation or that predictions will perform equally well on new learners.
In this simple regression with an intercept, R-squared equals the square of Pearson r from the same complete observations. Adding predictors can increase in-sample R-squared even when they offer little predictive value. Adjusted R-squared does not replace validation on appropriate held-out data.

title: Linear Regression
text:
7. Confidence intervals versus prediction intervals
A confidence interval describes uncertainty about the conditional mean score at a specified predictor value. A prediction interval describes uncertainty about a new individual score, including individual variation as well as estimation uncertainty.
new_learner <- data.frame(study_hours = 8)
predict(fit, newdata = new_learner, interval = "confidence")
predict(fit, newdata = new_learner, interval = "prediction")
The prediction interval is wider under the same model because a new learner may differ from the population mean. Both depend on the model assumptions and relevant predictor range. Neither describes a causal benefit from intervening on study hours.
The script’s grid uses observed study-hour limits. Its mean intervals are pointwise, not a simultaneous confidence band for the entire line. The dashed prediction limits are also pointwise intervals, not guaranteed coverage for every future learner simultaneously.

title: Linear Regression
text:
8. Adjusted associations and model specification
If prior score were measured before the study period, a prespecified model might be:
# Conceptual example only: prior_score is not in this chapter's dataset.
# adjusted <- lm(score ~ study_hours + prior_score, data = dat)
The study-hours coefficient would then describe its association with expected score holding prior score constant, under an additive linear model. Adjustment can change both the estimate and its uncertainty.
Choose covariates using the question, timing, and subject knowledge. Adding every available variable is not a general solution: adjusting for mediators or colliders can change the target or introduce bias. Collinearity can make individual coefficients unstable. An interaction means the slope depends on another variable, so a single common slope may be inappropriate.
This chapter’s runnable example fits only the one-predictor model. It does not claim to have controlled for prior ability or motivation.

title: Linear Regression
text:
9. Read the diagnostic figures

Residuals versus fitted: Look for systematic curvature and changing spread.
Normal Q-Q: Inspect departures from the normal-error approximation, especially tails.
Scale-location: Examine whether residual variability changes across fitted values.
Residuals versus leverage: Identify observations that may influence the fitted relationship.

Good-looking diagnostics cannot prove the model is correct or causal. Record important findings and explain how they affect inference. With n=16, avoid overconfidence in the apparent pattern.

11. Report your finding

In 16 synthetic learners, a simple linear regression estimated a positive association between study hours and assessment scores: 2.08 score points per additional hour (95% CI 1.54 to 2.62; two-sided p=0.000000873). The model’s sample R-squared was 0.832. Conventional inference assumes an appropriate linear mean structure and independent, normally distributed errors with constant variance. The model was unadjusted, and the association does not establish a causal study-time effect.

For applied reporting, add recruitment, missingness, diagnostic findings, model specification, sensitivity checks, and the intended scope of prediction or inference.

Adding variables solely to improve p-values
Prespecify a defensible model and record exploratory changes

2. When to use this method
Use binary logistic regression to model the conditional probability of a defined event using numerical or categorical predictors. Each observation’s outcome and predictors must be correctly aligned.
Independent Bernoulli observations are assumed in this example. Repeated outcomes, matched designs, clustered samples, and complex surveys need appropriate extensions or design-based methods. Counts, survival times, and unordered outcomes with several categories require other models.
Define whether the goal is describing an association, estimating an adjusted relationship, or predicting outcomes for new individuals. These goals require different choices about design, covariates, and validation.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
3. What it estimates or tests
If p is completion probability, its odds are \(p/(1-p)\). Logistic regression models log odds:
\[
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1X.
\]
The probability follows from the inverse-logit transformation:
\[
p=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1X)]}.
\]
For one additional session, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the modeled completion odds ratio, assuming a constant slope on the log-odds scale.

Slope null: \(\beta_1=0\), equivalent to an odds ratio of one.
Two-sided alternative: The slope differs from zero.

The script uses maximum-likelihood estimation and conventional asymptotic Wald inference. These calculations can be unreliable with sparse information, separation, or model misspecification.

4. Check before running







Check
What to establish

Independence
One independent learner per row, with clustering addressed if present


Missingness
Missing outcomes and predictors are investigated


Mean structure
Numerical predictor relationship is appropriate on the log-odds scale


Information
Enough events and non-events across predictor patterns for stable estimation


Separation
Predictor patterns do not perfectly or nearly determine the outcome


Influence and redundancy
Investigate influential cases and collinearity in larger models



Neither predictors nor binary outcomes need to be normally distributed. The linearity assumption concerns log odds, not a straight line in probability. Curves, transformations, or interactions may be needed for a suitable model.

Separation and convergence
Complete or quasi-complete separation can drive ordinary maximum-likelihood coefficients toward infinity. Warning signs include huge coefficients or standard errors, fitted probabilities near zero or one, and convergence warnings. Successful convergence alone does not guarantee stable estimates.
Do not ignore warnings or remove observations to manufacture convergence. Reconsider coding, information, and model complexity; suitable penalized or bias-reduced methods may be needed. No single events-per-variable rule guarantees an adequate model.

8. Adjustment and interpretation
With additional prespecified predictors, the session odds ratio would be conditional on those variables under the specified model. For example, prior experience could be relevant if appropriately measured before practice.
This dataset includes no adjustment variables. The runnable model is unadjusted and cannot support claims that it accounts for prior ability or motivation.
Choose covariates using the question, timing, and causal reasoning. Do not add every available variable or select solely by p-values. Logistic odds ratios are noncollapsible: adjusted and unadjusted odds ratios can differ even without confounding. A changed odds ratio alone does not prove that a variable was a confounder.

text:
9. Model checking and prediction performance
Inspect outcome counts across predictor values, plausible nonlinear patterns, residuals, leverage, and influence. Binary residuals do not behave like normal linear-regression residuals; do not require a normal residual Q-Q plot as a logistic assumption check.
A converged model and a small slope p-value do not establish predictive quality. For prediction, assess calibration and discrimination using appropriate validation, while preventing information leakage. An AUC alone does not establish well-calibrated probabilities, and a 0.5 classification threshold is not universally appropriate.
This teaching script fits the model and exports basic diagnostics. It does not perform external validation, a full calibration assessment, separation detection, or automated model selection.

The observed difference, A minus B, is -3 outcome units. Each group contains six independent participants. This deliberately small dataset allows complete permutation enumeration, but also makes bootstrap inference fragile.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods
text:
2. Two procedures, different purposes








Method
What changes?
Main purpose in this chapter




Bootstrap
Sample observations with replacement within each original group
Approximate sampling uncertainty of the mean difference


Permutation
Reallocate labels without replacement, preserving group sizes
Construct a null reference distribution



A bootstrap distribution is usually centered near the observed estimate. A null permutation distribution is centered near the null value for this symmetric allocation design. Do not interpret one as the other.
Neither method creates new independent information or repairs a biased sample. More resamples reduce simulation error, not the uncertainty caused by limited original data.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods
text:
3. Bootstrap uncertainty
For each bootstrap replicate:

Sample six A observations with replacement from A.
Independently sample six B observations with replacement from B.
Calculate the resampled mean A minus resampled mean B.

Repeat 19,999 times. The SD of those differences estimates the estimator’s SE. A percentile interval uses the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap estimates.
This is an approximate procedure, not an exact 95% guarantee. Small samples, bias, skewness, heavy tails, nonsmooth statistics, and boundary estimates can impair coverage. BCa, basic, and bootstrap-t intervals use different constructions and assumptions; do not call them interchangeable.
Resampling within groups preserves the two-group sampling structure without assuming their distributions are equal. Pooling before bootstrapping would change the procedure and its target uncertainty.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods
text:
4. Permutation null and exchangeability
The simple label-permutation procedure pools all 12 outcomes, selects six participant indices for A, and assigns the remaining six to B. There are:
\[
\binom{12}{6}=924
\]
possible allocations. Recalculate the difference for each allocation.
Under independent sampling from identical group distributions, labels are exchangeable under the null. Under an appropriate completely randomized assignment, the same allocation logic can provide a randomization test of a sharp no-effect null. State which justification applies to the actual study.
Equality of means alone does not generally justify unstudentized label permutation when distributions differ, such as unequal variances. A suitably studentized procedure can have useful asymptotic properties under weaker nulls, but is a different method and is not implemented here.
This example uses the absolute mean difference as its two-sided extremeness rule. All allocations with an absolute difference at least 3 count as extreme.

title: Bootstrap and Permutation Methods
text:
5. Match resampling to the design







Data structure
Design-aware consideration




Independent two-group observations
Bootstrap within groups; justify null label exchangeability


Paired outcomes
Bootstrap complete pairs; do not independently resample the two paired columns


Clustered participants
Resample independent clusters with an appropriate cluster-bootstrap procedure


Serial observations
Consider a suitable block bootstrap or time-series model


Restricted randomized assignment
Permute only assignments allowed by the design



Swapping labels within pairs or flipping difference signs requires its own null and symmetry or randomization justification. It is not an automatic paired-data solution.

    mean(sample(b, length(b), replace = TRUE))

For complete enumeration:
pooled <- c(a, b)
allocations <- combn(seq_along(pooled), length(a))
permuted <- apply(allocations, 2, function(index) {
  mean(pooled[index]) - mean(pooled[-index])
})
observed <- mean(a) - mean(b)
p_exact <- mean(abs(permuted) >= abs(observed) - 1e-12)

Monte Carlo permutation comparison
The script also draws 19,999 random label allocations with replacement across replicates and uses:
\[
\hat p_{MC}=\frac{b+1}{B+1},
\]
where b is the number of sampled statistics at least as extreme as observed and B is the number sampled. This standard plus-one construction avoids a zero p-value and supports valid randomized-test calibration under the appropriate exchangeability setup. It is not the formula for the fully enumerated calculation above.
The sampled estimate should be close to 0.03463, with simulation variation. The script reports the rough Monte Carlo SE \(\sqrt{\hat p_{MC}(1-\hat p_{MC})/B}\). This measures numerical simulation uncertainty, not uncertainty in the population effect.

In the bootstrap panel, the solid line marks the observed estimate and dashed lines mark the percentile interval limits. The distribution reflects repeated empirical sampling within the observed groups.
In the permutation panel, the null distribution is centered around zero. Dashed lines at -3 and +3 mark the two-sided extreme region. The p-value is determined by allocations in both tails, including equally extreme values.
A percentile interval is not obtained by reading the tails of this null permutation histogram. Nor should the fraction of ordinary bootstrap draws on either side of zero be automatically described as a valid null-test p-value.

12. Check your understanding
An AI tool pools A and B, resamples the pooled values, and calls the resulting difference interval an ordinary within-group bootstrap interval.
Why is this a different procedure?






Check your reasoning





Pooling replaces the separate empirical group distributions with a common one. It removes the observed group distinction from the resampling mechanism. title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text:
1. Your question
A study may compare several groups, examine multiple outcomes, or screen many features. Looking at many p-values increases opportunities for false rejection. This chapter uses six synthetic p-values to explain adjustment. They are teaching inputs, not outputs from an underlying dataset or real study.

title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text: How should we interpret evidence when several related hypotheses are tested?
crumbs: 21  Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons

title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text:
2. Define the family first
A testing family is the collection of hypotheses for which you intend a joint error-control claim. Define it using the scientific question, planned decisions, and analysis strategy before selecting favorable results.







Example
Possible family




All pairs among three groups
Three pairwise comparisons


Several outcomes supporting one intervention claim
Prespecified outcome tests relevant to that claim


Feature discovery in an omics screen
The prespecified set of tested features


One primary question plus exploratory analyses
Explicit primary and exploratory strategies, with justified error handling



Three groups produce \(3(3-1)/2=3\) pairs; five groups produce ten. Separate files or separate software runs do not automatically make hypotheses separate families.
Do not adjust only the p-values below 0.05, or split a family after seeing results. Adjustments cannot recover unrecorded model searches, outcome switching, or selective reporting.
crumbs: 21  Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons

title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text:
3. Choose the error-control goal








Goal
Definition
Example method




Family-wise error rate (FWER)
Probability of one or more false rejections in the family
Bonferroni or Holm


False discovery rate (FDR)
Expected false-discovery proportion among rejections, taking that proportion as zero when there are no rejections
Benjamini–Hochberg under suitable dependence conditions



FWER and FDR are different guarantees. FDR control at 5% does not mean every rejected hypothesis has a 5% probability of being false, nor that exactly 5% of a particular discovery list is false.
If 20 independent valid tests each have a 5% false-positive rate and all nulls are true, the chance of at least one false rejection is:
\[
1-(1-0.05)^{20}\approx0.642.
\]
The independence and all-null conditions matter; this calculation is not a universal false-discovery probability for every set of 20 tests.
crumbs: 21  Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons

title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text:
4. Understand the adjustments

Bonferroni
For m tests, compare each raw p-value with \(\alpha/m\), or use adjusted p-values \(\min(mp,1)\). With valid marginal p-values, it controls FWER under arbitrary dependence. It can be conservative.


Holm
Order the p-values from smallest to largest. Compare them sequentially with \(\alpha/(m-i+1)\), stopping at the first failure. Adjusted p-values use cumulative maxima of \((m-i+1)p_{(i)}\), capped at one, then return to the original order.
Holm controls FWER under arbitrary dependence when individual p-values are valid, and is never less powerful than ordinary Bonferroni for the same family.


Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)
Order the p-values and find the largest rank i satisfying:
\[
p_{(i)}\leq\frac{i}{m}q.
\]
Reject that hypothesis and all with smaller ordered p-values. Adjusted values use reverse cumulative minima of \(mp_{(i)}/i\), capped at one.
The usual FDR guarantee holds under independence and certain positive dependence conditions. Arbitrary dependence may require another procedure, such as Benjamini–Yekutieli, or a justified design-specific method. Do not assume that every correlated analysis meets BH’s conditions.

text:
7. Connect adjustment to follow-up analysis
An omnibus ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis result does not identify specific differing pairs. Use planned contrasts or an appropriate adjusted follow-up procedure. An omnibus rejection is not universal permission for unrestricted unadjusted comparisons.
Examples in earlier chapters include pairwise Welch tests with Holm adjustment, Tukey comparisons under a common-variance ANOVA model, and separate rank-sum tests with Holm adjustment. They use different assumptions and should be named accurately.
Prespecified contrasts can sometimes be tested without a preceding omnibus rejection under a valid planned strategy. Hierarchical or gatekeeping procedures need explicit rules; do not invent them after seeing p-values.

title: Multiple Testing and Follow-Up Comparisons
text:
8. Confidence intervals and effect sizes
Adjusted p-values do not adjust estimates, repair bias, or make small effects practically important. Report the effect estimate in meaningful units and describe uncertainty.
Ordinary 95% intervals for each comparison are not automatically simultaneous 95% intervals for the family. Holm-adjusted p-values can therefore accompany ordinary intervals that appear inconsistent with threshold decisions. Label the intervals clearly.
Bonferroni simultaneous intervals can be constructed using per-comparison confidence level \(1-\alpha/m\) when each interval has the required coverage. Tukey intervals supply a model-specific all-pairs simultaneous procedure. FDR-adjusted p-values do not automatically imply a corresponding set of ordinary intervals with a particular simultaneous coverage guarantee.

State the validity and dependence conditions for each guarantee. Do not filter to significant raw p-values before adjustment, choose the method based on discoveries, or interpret BH values as individual probabilities of false hypotheses.

Verify the family size, adjustment method, original row mapping, and intended error-control level. If AI generates additional outcomes, subgroups, transformations, or models during exploration, record that search and reconsider the scope of the claims. Multiplicity includes analytical choices, not just the final printed table.

10. Report your strategy and findings
For an applied family of confirmatory comparisons:

We prespecified the six hypotheses as one family and controlled the family-wise error rate at 0.05 using Holm’s procedure. We report all raw and adjusted p-values alongside estimates and clearly labeled intervals. In the synthetic adjustment example, only H1 met the Holm-adjusted threshold (adjusted p=0.018).

For exploratory discovery using BH, state the FDR target, family definition, dependence justification, and adjustment method. Describe findings as discoveries requiring contextual evaluation and, where appropriate, further validation. Do not claim that a particular proportion of the observed list is certainly false.

What should change?






Check your reasoning





The defined family contains six hypotheses. Selecting favorable values first changes the adjustment and invalidates the stated full-family guarantee. Apply the method to all six, retain their identities, and report the planned error-control goal and conditions.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
1. Your question
Before collecting data, specify the target difference, variability, design, testing procedure, and acceptable uncertainty. A software-generated sample size is only as defensible as those inputs.
This teaching example plans a two-sided, equal-allocation two-sample t-test with a common population SD. It is not a universal sample-size recommendation for educational studies.

title: Sample Size and Power
text: How many learners should we plan for to detect a meaningful difference between two independent population mean scores?

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
2. Define the planning inputs








Input
Illustrative choice
Why it matters




Outcome
Assessment score
Defines units and measurement


Meaningful mean difference
5 points
Difference the study should be able to detect


Assumed common SD
10 points
Determines noise relative to the target difference


Significance level
0.05
Type I error threshold for the planned test


Target power
80%
Rejection probability at the specified alternative


Alternative
Two-sided
Allows differences in either direction


Allocation
Equal groups
Same planned analyzable count in each arm


Expected loss fraction
15%
Illustrative recruitment allowance



Five points and SD ten are hypothetical assumptions, not estimates established by this guide. Use subject knowledge, prior evidence, and justified sensitivity ranges for an applied plan. A pilot SD can be highly uncertain.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
3. What power means
Power is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis if the specified alternative and model assumptions hold. It depends on the true effect, variability, sample size, test, and design.
An 80% target does not mean an 80% probability that the alternative is true, that this particular study will succeed, or that a significant finding will be correct. It describes repeated-sampling performance at a chosen alternative.
With the same design and variability, more independent observations usually increase power. Smaller target differences, greater variability, stricter alpha levels, and higher desired power generally require larger samples.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
4. Run the planning calculation
Copy the companion files into the repository root:

Illustrative planning assumptions
Complete base R script

Rscript scripts/R/22-sample-size.R
All chapter code blocks are non-executable. Run the standalone script separately.
plan <- power.t.test(delta = 5, sd = 10, sig.level = 0.05,
                     power = 0.80, type = "two.sample",
                     alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
ceiling(plan$n)
For type = "two.sample", n is per group, not the combined total. The function uses a common-variance t-test planning model. It does not directly calculate Welch power for arbitrary unequal variances or unequal allocation. Align the planning method with the intended analysis; use an appropriate extension or simulation when needed.
strict = TRUE includes rejection in both tails for the two-sided test. The script uses that setting consistently for planning and power verification.






Figure 22.1: Power versus analyzable independent participants per group under the specified five-point difference, SD ten, two-sided alpha 0.05, and equal-allocation t-test model. Reference lines mark target power and the rounded required sample size.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
5. Verify and explain the result
The calculation requires approximately 63.77 analyzable learners per group, rounded up to 64 per group, or 128 total, under the stated assumptions. The script recalculates power at the rounded integer sample size.
A rough large-sample check is:
\[
n\approx\frac{2\sigma^2(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})^2}{\Delta^2}.
\]
Substituting SD ten, difference five, alpha 0.05, and power 0.80 gives about 62.8 per group. The t-based result is slightly larger because it accounts for estimation of variance through the t distribution.

Allow for expected losses
An illustrative allowance is:
\[
n_{\text{recruit}}=\left\lceil\frac{n_{\text{analyzable}}}{1-L}\right\rceil.
\]
At 15% expected loss, \(\lceil64/0.85\rceil=76\) per group, or 152 recruits total.
This is an expected retention allowance, not a guarantee of 64 analyzable learners. It does not correct bias from informative dropout. Recruitment feasibility, differential losses, and missing-data handling need separate consideration.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
6. Examine sensitivity
The script recalculates required analyzable counts for assumed SDs of eight, ten, and twelve points. Inspect the exported sensitivity table instead of reporting a single count as certain.
Also consider plausible differences, target power levels, allocation ratios, and outcome quality. Do not choose an implausibly large effect or low variability merely to make the required sample affordable.
The power-curve figure shows power against analyzable participants per group for the fixed five-point, SD-ten model. It is conditional on those assumptions. It is not a probability forecast for an individual study.
The script generates 22-sample-size-plan.csv, 22-sd-sensitivity.csv, and 22-power-curve.csv under results/tables/, plus results/figures/22-power-curve.png. Pre-generated R outputs are not included; generate the files before rendering this chapter.

title: Sample Size and Power
section: 7. Precision can be the primary goal
text:
7. Precision can be the primary goal
Some studies primarily estimate a quantity rather than test a null. Plan around an acceptable confidence-interval width when that better matches the goal.
For an independent mean with a known planning SD, a rough normal-approximation count for desired half-width h is:
\[
n\approx\left(\frac{z_{0.975}\sigma}{h}\right)^2.
\]
This is a one-mean formula, not a two-group formula. Unknown variance, small samples, and complex designs need appropriate refinements. For proportions, planning precision depends on the anticipated proportion and interval method.
Avoid treating failure to reject as evidence of equivalence. Equivalence or noninferiority questions require a justified margin and a matching design and analysis.

title: Sample Size and Power
section: 8. Match the sample size to the independent unit
text:
8. Match the sample size to the independent unit







Design feature
Planning consequence




Learners within classrooms
Account for clustering and the number of classrooms


Paired measurements
Plan using variability of within-pair differences or an appropriate paired model


Repeated visits
Account for covariance, timing, and attrition


Several primary comparisons
Reflect the planned multiplicity strategy


Sparse binary outcomes
Ensure adequate event and non-event information for the intended model



For equal-sized clusters, the familiar approximation \(1+(m-1)ICC\) describes a design effect under a simple exchangeable correlation model. It is only a starting approximation; unequal cluster sizes, few clusters, allocation level, and degrees of freedom can materially change requirements.
Taking repeated measurements from the same participants does not produce the same information as recruiting that many independent participants. More rows cannot substitute automatically for more independent units.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
9. Avoid retrospective observed power
Do not calculate post-hoc power using the observed effect and interpret low power as an explanation of a nonsignificant p-value. For a fixed test and sample, observed-effect power often repackages the p-value and adds little useful information.
After analysis, emphasize the effect estimate and confidence interval. For a future study, use defensible external assumptions and sensitivity analyses. If a sample size is fixed by feasibility, report detectable effects or precision under several scenarios rather than claiming the sample is adequate without a target.
Repeatedly collecting data and stopping when p < 0.05 also changes error rates. Sequential designs need prespecified monitoring and appropriate inferential procedures.

title: Sample Size and Power
section: 10. Use AI and check its suggestions
text:
10. Use AI and check its suggestions

Plan an equal-allocation independent two-sample mean comparison with a meaningful difference of five score points, common SD ten, two-sided alpha 0.05, and target power 0.80. Use the stated common-variance t-test model and explain that n is per group. Round up, check achieved power, and calculate an illustrative 15% loss allowance. State that these are hypothetical assumptions, ask about clustering and missingness, and distinguish this model from unequal-variance Welch planning.

Verify units, independent unit, per-group versus total counts, rounding direction, loss denominator, and analysis compatibility. Ask for sensitivity calculations rather than a single unexplained number.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
11. Report the plan

Under an equal-allocation independent two-sample t-test planning model, detecting a five-point mean difference with common SD ten, two-sided alpha 0.05, and 80% power required 64 analyzable learners per group. An illustrative 15% loss allowance increased recruitment to 76 per group, or 152 total. These hypothetical inputs require substantive justification and sensitivity assessment before applied use; clustering and informative dropout are not addressed by this calculation.

An applied plan should identify evidence for every important input, the planned analysis, allocation, multiplicity handling, sensitivity range, feasibility, and reproducible software settings.

title: Sample Size and Power
text:
12. Check your understanding
An AI response says: “We need 64 learners total because power.t.test() returned n near 64.”
What should change?






Check your reasoning





For this two-sample calculation, n is per group. Round up to 64 analyzable learners in each group, giving 128 total before the illustrative loss allowance. Confirm the function’s model and the independent unit before using the count.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
1. Your task
A statistical report should answer the original question. Readers need the size and direction of the finding, its uncertainty, the relevant design and methods, and the limits of interpretation.
This chapter reuses Chapter 05’s synthetic independent-group scores to demonstrate a reproducible reporting workflow. It introduces no new statistical test.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text: Explain what the analysis found, how it was obtained, and what it does not establish.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
2. Start with an evidence summary
Before writing, assemble the information needed to support the claim.







Element
What to record




Question
Population, outcome, comparison, and target quantity


Design
Independent, paired, repeated, clustered, or another structure


Data
Source, units, sample sizes, exclusions, and missingness


Method
Test or model, alternatives, reference categories, and key assumptions


Estimate
Magnitude, direction, and meaningful units


Uncertainty
Interval level and construction; test result when relevant


Diagnostics
Checks performed, findings, and consequential problems


Multiplicity
Family, adjustment, and planned versus exploratory analyses


Limitations
Bias, confounding, imprecision, generalizability, and design restrictions


Reproducibility
Input version, script, software environment, and output paths



Do not invent missing design details to make a paragraph sound complete. Mark unresolved facts and investigate them before applied reporting.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
3. Use a short results structure
A useful sequence is:

Describe the analyzed sample and relevant group summaries.
State the estimate and its direction in units the reader understands.
Report an appropriate interval and, where relevant, the test statistic and p-value.
Answer the question with uncertainty and design limitations.

A general writing template is:

Among [analyzed units], [descriptive summary]. The estimated [target quantity], defined as [direction], was [estimate and units] ([interval level and method] CI [limits]). [Specified test or model] yielded [statistic, degrees of freedom if applicable, p-value and adjustment status]. These results [careful answer], with limitations from [relevant issues].

Adapt the template to the actual method. An exact test may have no familiar t statistic or degrees of freedom to report. Do not force every analysis into identical fields.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
4. Worked reporting example



Quantity
Synthetic result




Group A
n=20; mean 69.30; SD 6.97


Group B
n=20; mean 74.10; SD 13.96


Mean difference, A minus B
-4.80 points


95% Welch confidence interval
-11.95 to 2.35 points


Welch t statistic
-1.376


Approximate df
27.91


Two-sided p-value
0.1798



A suitable results paragraph is:

In the synthetic example, mean assessment scores were 69.30 points (SD 6.97, n=20) in A and 74.10 points (SD 13.96, n=20) in B. The estimated mean difference, A minus B, was -4.80 points (95% Welch CI -11.95 to 2.35). A two-sided Welch t-test gave t(27.91)=-1.38, p=0.1798. The interval includes zero and potentially important differences; these results do not establish equivalence or a causal group effect.

For a less technical audience:

The sample mean was 4.8 points lower in A than in B. The uncertainty interval ranged from about 12 points lower to 2.3 points higher. The data do not give a precise answer about the population difference, and this comparison alone does not show that either approach caused a change in scores.

These paragraphs summarize a teaching calculation. A real report must include the actual sampling process, diagnostic findings, missing-data handling, and relevant study context.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
5. Separate methods, results, and interpretation








Section
Purpose
Example content




Methods
Explain what was planned and done
Independent-unit design, outcome definition, Welch test, interval level, missingness strategy


Results
Present observed summaries and estimates
Group means, A-minus-B difference, interval, and p-value


Discussion
Explain meaning and limitations
Practical importance, uncertainty, possible bias, and scope of claims



Record departures from the plan and why they occurred. Label exploratory findings and sensitivity analyses. Do not rewrite the methods as if an outcome-driven decision had been prespecified.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
6. Report numbers consistently
Use enough precision to support interpretation without implying unrealistic accuracy. Keep units and comparison direction consistent across text, tables, code, and figures.

Report an SD for individual variation and an SE or interval for estimate uncertainty; do not interchange them.
State whether an interval is ordinary, simultaneous, bootstrap, Wald, exact conditional, or another construction.
Label adjusted p-values with the method and comparison family.
Avoid p=0.000. Use suitable scientific notation or a clearly stated reporting threshold.
Distinguish percentage points from relative percentage changes.
Distinguish odds ratios, proportion ratios, and absolute differences.

A 95% confidence interval describes the long-run performance of its procedure under assumptions. It does not generally assign a 95% probability to the fixed parameter lying within the observed interval.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
section: 7. Choose language that matches the evidence
text:
7. Choose language that matches the evidence







Avoid
More defensible wording




“There was no difference” solely because p > 0.05
“The interval includes zero and differences that may matter; the estimate is uncertain”


“The result proves the intervention works”
“The result supports [specific claim] under the design and analysis assumptions”


“X causes Y” from an observational association
“X was associated with Y,” with potential confounding explained


“The result was significant,” with no magnitude
Report the estimate, interval, and practical context


“The groups are equivalent” after a nonsignificant ordinary test
Explain that equivalence needs a justified margin and appropriate procedure


“AI verified the result”
Describe the checks actually performed by the analyst and software



A small p-value does not establish a large or useful difference. A large p-value does not establish absence. Keep the estimate, uncertainty, and decision context together.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
8. Make figures and tables interpretable
Use figures when they clarify distributions, relationships, or uncertainty. Show individual observations where suitable, preserve pairing visually when relevant, and state units and denominators.
For interval plots, explain what the dot and interval represent. Distinguish mean confidence intervals from individual prediction intervals. Avoid significance stars as the only explanation of evidence.
A table should identify the sample or denominator, estimate, direction, interval construction, and adjustment status. State whether descriptive summaries use all available observations or the same analysis sample as the inferential result.

Copy these companion files into the repository root:

Pre-generated R outputs are not included or required for chapter rendering. Review the generated paragraph before publication; software cannot infer unrecorded design details or substantive limitations.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
section: 10. Use AI and check the draft
text:
10. Use AI and check the draft

Using only the supplied evidence table and verified study notes, draft a concise methods description and results paragraph. Preserve the A-minus-B direction, units, sample sizes, interval method, and p-value. Separate observed findings from interpretation. Identify missing facts instead of inventing them. Do not turn a nonsignificant test into equivalence or an association into causation. List every numerical statement so I can check it against the exported results.

Check every number against the saved output, every claim against the design, and every reference against its actual source. Keep track of consequential AI suggestions and revisions. Follow applicable institutional or publication requirements for disclosing AI assistance.
Use synthetic data or authorized de-identified summaries when seeking drafting help. A fluent paragraph is not evidence that the underlying calculation or claim is correct.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
11. Review before sharing
Ask yourself:

Can the reader identify the question and independent unit?
Are estimates, units, direction, and uncertainty correct?
Are missingness, exclusions, and analysis changes documented?
Are assumptions and diagnostic findings described accurately?
Is multiplicity handled and labeled where relevant?
Does the interpretation distinguish association, prediction, and causation?
Can another person trace the paragraph to the inputs, script, and outputs?

Resolve discrepancies between figures, tables, and text before sharing. Preserve the exact output version used in the report.

title: Reporting Statistical Findings
text:
12. Check your understanding
An AI draft changes “A minus B was -4.80 points” to “A improved scores by 4.80 points compared with B.”
Which claims changed?






Check your reasoning





The draft reverses the direction: the original estimate indicates a lower mean in A. It also introduces improvement over time and a causal effect, neither established by this independent-group comparison. Restore the signed estimate, interval, and design-appropriate wording.

Appendix B: Design reminders







Term
Practical meaning




Independent unit
A participant, plot, cluster, or other unit supplying independent information


Paired measurements
Two observations linked by the same unit or justified matching


Repeated measurements
Several observations from the same unit


Clustered observations
Units sharing a higher-level grouping that may induce dependence


Random sampling
A sampling mechanism supporting inference to a specified population


Random assignment
An allocation mechanism supporting a treatment comparison under additional conditions



Random assignment and random sampling serve different purposes. Neither can be inferred from the appearance of the data table. Unique identifiers do not prove independence.

text:
Appendix C: Glossary







Term
Meaning




Parameter
A quantity defined for a population or statistical model


Estimator
A rule for estimating a parameter from data


Estimate
The value obtained by applying that rule


Standard deviation
Variation among observations


Standard error
Sampling variability of an estimator under the specified design and model


Confidence interval
An interval procedure with a stated long-run coverage property under assumptions


Prediction interval
An interval for a new observation under a specified prediction model


P-value
Probability under the null and other test assumptions of a statistic at least as extreme as observed, under the stated extremeness rule


Effect size
Magnitude of a difference or relationship, in original or standardized units


Odds
Event probability divided by one minus that probability


Percentage-point difference
Absolute difference between percentages


Confounding
Distortion of an intended relationship by other variables in the causal structure


Exchangeability
Invariance of a joint distribution to specified relabelings under the relevant model or design


Sphericity
Equal variances of pairwise contrasts for the repeated conditions in the standard setting


FWER
Probability of at least one false rejection within a family


FDR
Expected false-discovery proportion, defined as zero when there are no rejections


Power
Probability of rejecting the null at a specified alternative under a design and test


Sensitivity analysis
Examination of how conclusions change under justified alternative assumptions or decisions
